Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 113, to amend the Bills of Exchange Act.
He said: This is a .very simple amendment, but it is considered of very great importance from the point of view of the banking business of the country. It is to amend the present provision to the effect that no protest of a bill of exchange can take place until three o'clock in the afternoon by substituting half-past two. It is represented by the bankers generally that as a result of the large number of their employees who have been called away for military service, it is very difficult for them indeed to have the necessary work after the closing hour of the bank done in the day by the employees who are with them, and that it would mitigate that inconvenience very greatly if it were possible for them to close hanking hours at half-past two instead of three o'clock. If the House would be disposed to give consent to the introduction of the Bill without notice- which, of course, would imply the waiving of the rules as to the different readings-
I would beg for leave to introduce Bill No. 113, to amend the Bills of Exchange Act. Of course, I understand that if it cannot be dealt with in that way, it cannot be dealt with at all.

I understand that the Bill of which my hon. friend has given notice of his intention to introduce, is, as represented, a very important one. It has been represented to me also that the banking staffs have been so depleted by the necessities of the military service that it is impossible for them to do their work within the usual hours. Therefore the Bill becomes a public necessity. It can inconvenience nobody. It is simply to provide that bills of exchange may be protested at half-past-two instead of three o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

speakeroldname: Hon. N. W. ROWELL (President of the Council):
subtopic: CIVIL PAY OF CIVIL SERVANTS ' OVERSEAS.
speechtext:
The Prime Minister stated yesterday that an announcement would be made to-day with reference to the civil pay of civil servants serving overseas, and I now wish to read to the House the operative part of an Order in Council passed on the 21st of May dealing with this matter. The members of the House will recall that there are three classes into which the civil servants who are now serving with the military forces might be divided: Those who went overseas in the early part of the war received both their civil pay and their
2.386

military pay. At a later day an Order in Council was passed providing that those who enlisted after that date should receive whichever pay was the larger of the two, civil or military, and then, when the Military Service Act came into operation, an Order in Council was passed providing that civil servants enlisting after that date would receive their military pay only. By the Order in Council of the 5th of April, 1918, those Orders in Council were all modified so as to provide that, after the date fixed in that Order in Council, civil servants would receive only their military pay. The present Order in Council repeals the last Order in Council and substitutes the following provisions:
1.	The above mentioned Orders in Council- Those are, the first Order in Council which provided for both civil and military pay for those who enlisted in the earlier part of the war; the second Order in Council which provided for the larger pay of the two for those who enlisted subsequently, and the third Order in Council which provided simply for the military pay:
1.	The above-mentioned Orders in Council shall continue to apply in respect of any person in the civil employment of the Government absent upon service with the forces of His Majesty or of any of His Miajesty's Allies and who
(a)	is now serving in any theatre of actual war outside of the United Kingdom, so long as so serving, or
(b)	is now or who may be hereafter in the United Kingdom and who has served1 in such theatre of actual war outside thereof and is there detained by reason of wounds or disease received or contracted in such service, so long as so detained, or
(c)	is now or who may be hereafter in the United Kingdom and who has served in such theatre of actual war outside thereof and has suffered from wounds or disease received or contracted in such service and is undergoing preparation in a reserve battalion for return to said theatre of actual war, or
(d)	is now in the United Kingdom and who has served in such theatre of actual war outside thereof for at least one year and has been brought back to the United Kingdom for military duty and is still required for military duty there.
2.	A prisoner of war shall he deemed to be serving in a theatre of actual war outside of the United Kingdom and shall come within the provision of Clause (a) of section 1 of this Order.
3.	All other persons in the civil employment of the Government absent upon service with the forces of His Majesty shall from and after the 15th day of-July, 1918, receive only military pay, anything in the above recited Orders in Council to the contrary notwithstanding.
4.	Any person in the civil employment of the Government absent upon service with the forces of His Majesty, or any of His Majesty's Allies, shall be entitled upon the conclusion of the latter service, to be restored to his position

in the civil employment of the Government, if he remains qualified to discharge the duties appertaining to that position.
5.	The Order in Council of April 5th, 1918, (P. C. 811) is hereby revoked and cancelled.
The net result of this Order in 'Council is to continue the existing Orders in Council in force in respect of all civil servants now serving in the forces of His Majesty or His Majesty's Allies except those in Canada and those in the United Kingdom who have not seen real service at the front.

/Bill No. 107, to incorporate the United Canadian Insurance Company-.Sir Herbert Ames-Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-incorporation :
May I ask the Chairman of the Banking and Commerce Committee, to which this Bill was referred, to give an explanation?

By the unanimous consent of the House, in order to ensure the passing of this Bill, it has been placed on the Orders of to-day, It was passed by the Banking and Commerce Committee this morning, having been unduly delayed because of the necessity of changing the name of the company as it first appeared asking for incorporation, namely, the British Canadian Insurance Company, as that name had

already been, appropriated by a company authorized by the legislature of the province of Quebec. Hon. members who were in this House four or five years ago will remember that there was what might be called a model or standard Insurance Bill passed by the Banking and Commerce Committee, and afterwards ratified by this House, and since that time the condition has always been imposed upon any company desiring incorporation that their Act of Incorporation should conform with the model or standard Bill. The Bill before us does not deviate by a single word from the model Bills which we have passed through this House on many occasions during the last two or three years incorporating new insurance companies. The only thing that would strike any one is the fact that section 1 incorporates a firm of Ottawa lawyers as an insurance company.
Owing to the illness of one of the incorporators and the difficulty of getting the signatures, it was found impossible to get the signatures of the men who are really behind this Bill in time for it to pass this session. I am informed that the real promoters of the Bill are H. S. Durkee, P. F. Wright, J. Kendall, O. S. Wood, and A. G. Creelman, all well known citizens of Vancouver, whose signatures could not be obtained in time. Consequently, the formality has been adopted of putting the Bill through in the name of the firm in which Mr. W. L. Scott, K.C., is a chief member. That was the only point of criticism. The Banking and Commerce Committee and the department were satisfied on that point and the Bill was unanimously passed this morning without amendment.

Do I understand that this incorporation is sought to replace another company and was there any objection to the name? Do I also understand that there was no objection before the Banking and Commerce Committee and that it went through unanimously?

The hon. member (Mr. Bureau) does not quite understand what happened. The Bill, as it was first passed in the Senate was to incorporate the British Canadian Insurance Company. Before the Senate it was pointed out that there was already a company under that name that had been incorporated by the Legislature of Quebec. Objection coming from that source, the original promoters of this Bill undertook to alter their name. That has caused the delay. This Bill would
have been through the House before this had it not been for that fact.

Would the hon. gentleman (Sir Herbert Ames), who is the chairman of the committee, be good enough to give us any (reason why the House should take up this Bill without a copy of it in our hands or any other information?
I do not think this Bill should go on for a second.
Copies of the Bill are procurable and may be distributed if desired.
I think these gentlemen ought to know what the rules are with regard to signatures and, if they have not got them in, this House should not be asked to adopt the procedure that is proposed here.
The main object of the Bill is to incorporate this company to enable it to do hail insurance before the present heavy crop in the western provinces is subject to danger of destruction by hail.
I thought these gentlemen came from Vancouver?

That is the excuse offered for asking that this company be immediately incorporated. I understand from the promoters that there is British capital ready to be placed behind the company to the necessary extent to enable them to do a bail insurance business.
I thought this was a Vancouver company?
It is.
What has it to do with crops?

There is no reason why any Vancouver, Toronto, or Halifax company should not be incorporated to do hail insurance or many other lines of insurance in the Dominion. The members of the committee understand that there is a great variety of insurance business, and that when a new insurance company is incorporated, it as compelled to indicate the order in which it shall do the different classes of insurance; for instance the first, the second, the third, the fourth and so on. It is compelled to have a certain amount of capital subscribed and a certain amount of capital paid up before it can undertake the first class of insurance business, a certain amount of capital paid up before it can undertake the second class of insurance,

and so on with regard to the third and the fourth classes of business. A company oftentimes does six or eight different kinds of business, and it increases the amount of subscribed capital and the amount paid up in proportion to the increase and extent of the business carried on. This company, at present, desires to engage in hail insurance. It will be extended, if it can secure the necessary capital, .to fire insurance, cyclone insurance, and other classes of insurance. The promoters are anxious to be incorporated early so that the company can take advantage of the very large crops which are expected in the West, to engage in hail insurance.
Is this company now doing any other insurance than hail insurance?
The hon. gentleman will find that in clause 5 of the Bill.
I have just got a copy of the Bill now.
My hon. friend will find that it is incorporated to do ten classes of insurance, one after another as its capital and deposits increase.

May I ask the hon. gentleman whether or not there are companies in the West doing what is known as an exclusive hail insurance business? If so, I would like to know whether he thinks it is fair to put in competition with them a company dealing in various classes of insurance. The reason I ask that question is that complaints have come from well known insurance companies that American insurance companies have come into this country and employed the profits they are making on ~ other branches of insurance to enable them to give lower rates than the Canadian insurance companies can give for hail or weather insurance. I just raise the point as to whether there would be anything unfair in that clause as affecting the rights of thoroughly weather and hail insurance companies operating in the west.

I am informed by the promoters of the Bill that the first board of directors will all be Canadians and that the shareholders will be Canadians and persons residing in Great Britain, where they expect to secure a por-t;on of their capital. As to the other question of hail insurance, perhaps some of the ministers, from the West, probably the hon. the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Crerar), or the hon. the Minister of Customs (Mr. Sifton), or the hon. the Min-
ister of Immigration (Mr. Calder), could explain better than I about hail insurance in the West.
Do I understand that this company is now in existence and has been carrying on business in any of these capacities?
No.

I think it is most extraordinary that a firm of lawyers in the city of Ottawa should get a charter like this. What is to prevent them from going out into the open market and selling or hawking about that charter? It is a very peculiar transaction and I do not think the House should agree to it.

We were assured in the committee this morning by Mr. W. L. Scott, who is a well known and responsible lawyer of the city of Ottawa, that he had no direct interest in it further than a lawyer working for his clients, that he had no intention of selling the charter or doing anything of the kind, and that he was securing it for these gentlemen whom I have mentioned at their request. He put before the committee proof of the fact that he was acting merely for them in his capacity as a parliamentary agent.
Did he show urgent need for this Bill?
He convinced the committee to that effect.
Do the rules of the House require the signatures of the applicants for a charter?
Yes.
Is it not possible to get by telegraph the authority of these gentlemen to use their names?

That authority was put before the committee this morning in the form of telegrams from Vancouver. The signatures of these five gentlemen whom I have mentioned wea-e all in the petition and everything is perfectly regular as fir as that is concerned. We were shown this morning telegrams from these five gentlemen that I spoke of, authoiizing the use of their names as directors and shareholders of the company.

There would be no objection if the House deems it adv.sab'e to put in the names of the five Canadian gentlemen whose names I have given. That was discussed in the committee this morning, the only objection being that it would require the Bill to go back to the Senate, and it might possibly fall by the wav'side before prorogation. It would be quite in order for the House to insert the names of the five gentlemen, thus making ten altogether, of whom five, at least, are well known Canadian citizens.

It is the practice in the case of letters patent under the Joint Stock Companies' Act for solicitors to take out charters and only the names of the solicitors, their clerks and stenographers are used. But I think that in the case of a parliamentary application it has generally been considered advisable that the real promoters of the enterprise should have their names in the Bill. J have no doubt that the proceeding is all right, and I am quite sure that the name of Mr. Scott is a guarantee of good faith, but if the names of the real promoters were put in the Bill it would .be desirable. I do not say any more than that.

I understand that
facts have been brought out this morning that were not disclosed before the Banking and Commerce Committee. The statement that the chairman has given about a change in the name of the company was never presented to the Banking and Commerce Committee.
Sir HERBERT AMiES:	Yes, it was.
Sir S.AIM HUGHES:	I am informed it
was not.
Everything mentioned by me this morning was brought out before the Banking and Commerce Committee.

What is complained of may be irregular, but it is a very common practice in taking out letters patent and no harm has resulted from it, and no harm will result in any event. I did not raise any objection in the Banking and Commerce Committee and I do not propose to do so now. I do not see why the Bill should be delayed at all for the reasons assigned.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall clause 1 carry?
No, lost.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Carried.
On section 2-Provisional directors.

Surely, Mr. Chairman, you are going to accept the proposition of the hon. member for Queens and Shelburne (Mr. Fielding) in regard to the substitution of these gentlemen's names. It is a very dangerous practice to insert the name of a firm of lawyers into a Bill in the manner proposed. This jobbing in parliamentary charters is an old practice round Ottawa, and I certainly think it should not be encouraged by this House in the closing hours of the session. The crop might be hailed out anyway before these gentlemen are ready to operate this year, and we may possibly save money by not passing this Bill. It strikes me, and has always done so, that proceedings such as this at the tail-end of the session are very peculiar- they resemble a deathbed repentance. I think this Bill should stand over until next session, and. in any event the names of the other gentlemen interested should be added. I would go further and say substitute their names for the names of the lawyers which appear in the Bill. The lawyers in question form a large firm and it takes a lot to keep them going.

I might say that, speaking for the province of Saskatchewan, in so far as hail insurance is concerned, it does not make any difference whether this Bill goes through or not. If the Bill passes, the provincial authorities will see to it that the company is properly organized, has the proper standing, and afford the necessary capital proper security before they will allow it to do business in that province.
That is the rule of all the provinces.

It is the rule in Saskatchewan, and I understand it is also the rule in the province of Alberta. In some of the western provinces they have had somewhat unfortunate experiences with regard to these hail insurance companies, as a result of which the law was put into such shape that no company can do business unless it has proper standing and provides the proper security.
On.section 6-increase of capital-
Has the Minister of Immigration and Colonization read clause 6 of the Bill, and is he satisfied with it?
I have not seen the Bill.
It strikes me that the increase of capital provided for in that clause for each line of business is rather light.

The increases are such as .appear in other Bills that have been adopted, with 'the single exception of burglary insurance, where the capital is made $20,000 instead of $10,000, since the liability is regarded as slightly greater than it would otherwise 'be. With that exception, the increases are the same as have been granted in the case of about a score of other Bills.

I agree with what has
been said 'by the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton, and I would like to say further that this Bill does not seem to have been distributed to all the members. I also wish to call the attention of the Clerk of the House to the fact that the Printing Bureau appears to have sent an insufficient number of Bills and papers to the House in certain .cases. For example, the other day when the Supplementary Estimates arrived there were not sufficient to place a copy of each in the box of each member, as custom and usage requires. In the present case there are apparently only a few copies of the Bill obtainable, and there has not been one placed on my file. If, as has been stated, this Bill was at first given a wrong, title, the proper procedure would have 'been to send the petition to the committee, where the change could have been made and the Rill would then go through in proper form. I have in mind the case of a number of gentlemen in British Columbia who got into trouble over an insurance Bill, in consequence of which the Bill in question was- thrown out by the committee. I would like to know whether those gentlemen are associated with this Bill, and if so, whether they are trying to get through an objectionable Bill in the dying hours of the session? If we are going to adhere to parliamentary procedure I think the objections raised to this Bill will be fatal to it. Had the proper procedure been adopted in respect to this Bill the names of the promoters would have remained on it. Instead of that the Bill was withdrawn for some reason, and a new measure introduced, which contains the names of certain lawyers. I hardly think that is fair to the House.

The hon. gentleman is under a slight misapprehension in this matter. This Bill was considered by the Private Bills 'Committee and the Banking and Commerce Committee of the Senate when it was pointed out that the name of this company had been already used in another case. The Banking and Commerce Committee of 'the Senate thereupon arranged 
for a new title and reported to the Senate that it was advisable to have the existing name changed. That necessarily caused some delay in the Bill coming from the *Senate and accounts for it arriving here at a somewhat late period. When the Bill reached this House-its title was exactly as printed, " United Canadian Insurance Company " (E2). There has not been any change in a word or a syllable of the Bill since it first appeared in this House.
Mr. OURR'IE: What is the reason the names of the original promoters do not appear on the Bill?

The names of the original promoters were not attached to the original petition, owing to the illness of the person to whom that petition was entrusted,
* when it was presented to the Senate in sufficient time to appear in the Bill. This is the explanation that is given to us. >
I may say that the Banking and Commerce Committee were unanimously satisfied of the bona fides of Mr. W. L. Scott and his associates and felt that there would be no danger in granting a Bill of this character. It was shown to us that there was very urgent need of additional hail insurance facilities in the western provinces this summer, where the crop is the largest and most valuable ever put in the ground; and that it would be advisable to permit another company to do business there this summer along these lines.

It strikes me that this very important Bill comes to us in a very hasty way, and at a time when we are not able to give very much consideration to it. It may have been very seriously considered in the Senate, and it may be all right. But the insurance business is a very important business, second to banking, I suppose, perhaps the most important business that any body of men are permitted to carry on in this country. When we are authorizing people to carry on insurance business in this country, we should know something about it. I would like to ask the Acting Minister of Finance in whose department these matters particularly lie, if he is satisfied that this concern is a strong, reliable set of men, and that if busineess is (put in their hands the interests of the country are safe? The hon. Minister of Immigration and Colonization has suggested a point of law on whieh I am not at all satisfied. He says that there is a guarantee for the people of Alberta against the operations of such companies by reason of the protections that local laws give them.

As ^ lawyer, I am not satisfied that the local legislature could estop an insurance company chartered by this House from doing business in the province of Alberta. If there is/ a decision of the Supreme Court of Canada to that effect I shall be very glad to hear it. But it strikes me that there is no jurisdiction in the local legislature to estop the operations of a corporation chartered to do business by this House all over the country. There may be, but I am not familiar with it. And if that is the only protection which the people of Alberta and the different provinces have, I am not satisfied. And I am not satisfied that sufficient time has been given to this Bill. I agree entirely with the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) that there is no such haste about it, and that this Bill could very well stand over.

I do not want to hold up the Bill except on square lines. I call attention that it is not printed in French. And as an ardent lover of the French language, the House is entitled to have this Bill printed in French. Furthermore, I would ask the opinion of the Minister of Customs, who is reputed to be a shrewd lawyer, well up on matters affecting this class of insurance in the West, and upon the question of rates. I would like an opinion from him in that regard.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The Minister of Justice
gives the legal advice for this Government, and I would not for a moment wish to infringe upon his prerogatives. I have no legal advice to give in regard to the constitutional privileges as they are affected by this particular Act. I do not think it will lower the rate of insurance any. I do not think it will make any difference so far as that is concerned. There are lots of hail insurance companies in the western provinces. However, I have no objection to any new company. I have never known any of these companies who are prepared to do business with farmers on any better terms than the others. They are all alike when it comes to doing business.

In answer to the question put to me by the member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie), I have given no personal attention to the Bill; but I am assured by the officers of the department that it is in no respect objectionable. The Bill in its terms follows the standard clauses usually inserted in Bills incorporating insurance companies. Some Bills have been introduced in the past in the very
same terms. I do not see any objection to this Bill.
Is it a bona fide company, that is the point? Where is there any evidence that this is a bona fide company? A firm of lawyers may wish, inasmuch as the law business is not very brisk now-
Louder.
I am glad to see my legal friend pricking up.

I would like to hear
what the gallant member is saying about the profession.

The point I want to make is this. I am only looking at one aspect of the case-we must look at it from every aspect. Business being a little dull in law offices possibly, a legal firm might take up the incorporation of such a company. They get up a charter of this kind. We have had instances in Canada where charters have been passed in this House and hawked around for sale. This Rill has all the earmarks of that sort of a charter. Surely if a number of gentlemen -I did not catch the names; they were muttered in an undertone,-from Vancouver are so solicitous in looking after the farmers of the Western prairies, why did they not get this Bill down in time? They have had all summer to look into this matter. They are coming down at the eleventh hour, without even the signatures of the parties, and the legal firm are getting them by telegraph. The thing looks fishy on the face of it. It can very well stand over for another session; there is no great rush. Furthermore, the number of functions inserted would require a considerable amount to be put up for going into classes of insurance other than hail insurance. These things, to my mind, are altogether insufficient.
I was a member of the Banking Committee which sat on this matter this morning. I would tell this Committee that Mr. Scott, who is a lawyer of standing in Ottawa-
Are not all lawyers lawyers of standing?
No, they vary. There are, sad to say, lawyers who do not rise to the general high level maintained by the profession. I have heard of newspaper men of the same sort, and doctors of the same sort.
And soldiers.

Oh, no. Soldiers are always noble and great, of the very highest calibre. I would like to say this: I do not see why we cannot pass this Bill. Mr. Scott assured us that it was a bona fide Bill, that his clients in Vancouver and Victoria were bona fide people of responsibility. He showed correspondence to that effect. Under these circumstances, I would ask'the hon. and gallant member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes), with, that disregard of red tape which was a distinguishing characteristic of his in days gone by, not to insist on red tape now, but as we are all desirous of going on with more important business we might possibly be allowed to pass this Bill and get on to other matters. I speak with all of the deference and respect due from a young member of this House to an old member like my hon. friend.

I would ask the hon. member in charge of the Bill if the preliminary proceedings, the notices in the Canada Gazette, were taken in the names of these men, or the names of the proposed bona fide promoters?
I understand they were issued in the name of W. L. Scott and his associates.
That is a rather suspicious circumstance to me.

I think the answer-
' Some hon. MEMBERS: Order.

If the original proceedings and notices were put through in the names of these incorporators, it does not look very feasible that men who really -were the bona fide incorporators at the inception of the movement would lend the scheme out to the use of other names. That is suspicious to my mind, and makes me wonder if somebody has been putting one over on the hon. member who is in charge of the Bill. I think Mr. Scott is a reputable gentleman, but it must be noticed that he is one of the promoters, and it sounds a little like a man praising himself in a measure, when all the information the Banking Committee receives has been received from one of the promoters himself. If the Bill from' its inception was put forward in the name of this firm of solicitors, it is a strange thing to me; it does not show good faith. The excuse is given that the actual signatories could not be obtained because the men in question are in Vancouver.
rMr. McMaster.!
Signatories to what?

The petition. These pretended incorporators must have made up their minds weeks ago with regard to this matter. They must have entered into a memorandum of agreement to form the company; their names must be on all the preliminaries, Yet the names of Ottawa . lawyers are given here as the promoters of the company. It does not look like good faith; it looks like a policy of huckstering charters.
Mr. GURE-IE: 'If the member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) had been in the House for several years he would have known that some trouble has been experienced with companies from Vancouver. Last session we had a very bad case. A charter wras obtained some years ago in this form and the parties who received it started out to get a large number of subscriptions. It was ascertained that a large amount that had been paid in as subscriptions had been taken by way of commissions. Nothing was left but a shell for the creditors of the company; and the company never went into operation. I do not object to charters being granted to promoters in Vancouver but we should look into the bona tides of these cases. The memler from the section of the country in which this company is to operate should be in his place to speak on behalf of these incorporators and to say that they are all right. If any member from Vancouver or British Columbia does that I will withdraw all objection.
The member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) is really the promoter of the Bill; but he is not here to-day.

His name does not appear on the Bill.
Sir HERBERT AMiES: It is a matter of record that he is the promoter of the Bill in this House.
Mr. 'CURRIE: Somebody ought to be here to explain the matter, because the case of last year, to which I referred, was a flagrant one. There is also the principle of charter-mongering, to which I object. This is a very important insurance company; their powers are almost as wide as Lloyd's, and we should not be obliged to accept simply the ipse dixit of the Ottawa lawyers whose names have been given. If the Secretary of State (Hon. Mr. Burrell) will say that the Bill is all right, we will let it go at that

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Frankly, I know nothing whatever about the Bill. If, however, the member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) knows the promoters of the Bill, I should think that would be sufficient.

Would the public receive any greater protection by the fact that the member for Vancouver is the sponsor of the Bill? What difference does that make? The public must be protected by the insurance laws of the country and their proper administration by the Insurance Department,

We have rules in
this House that we are asked to observe, and I always observe them to the utmost limit of the law, even when they are stretched beyond the point of endurance. This is one case in which the rules should be carefully observed. I know the business men of Vancouver pretty well and I should like to hear again the names of the promoters and to know what business they are engaged in. It looks fishy, toi use a not very decorous expression; it looks peculiar to see the names of the promoters of this Bill furnished from a law office in Ottawa. The names of the men from Vancouver are telegraphed, not sent by letter; the whole thing looks peculiar, to say the least.

I shall be glad
to give the names again. H. S. Durlree, who, I understand is a railway man; P. F. Wright, grocer; J. Kendall, whose designation I cannot give; O. S. Wood, who, I think, is a lawyer, and A. G. Creelman, contractor. If t'he hon. member will refer to the Orders of the Day of May 20th he will find that Bill 107 (letter E of the Senate) an Act to incorporate the United Canadian Insurance Company was introduced that day by the member for Vancouver Centre (iM'r. Stevens). The Bill was unanimously passed this morning by the Banking and Commerce Committee, and I am in charge of it for the member for Vancouver Centre.

Does the Secretary
of State know whether these gentlemen are in good standing in Vancouver?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I know Mr. Creelman; I do not know the other gentlemen, although I have heard their names occasionally. I knew Mr. Creelman as a contractor in the Kootenay railroad district; he is a man of some substance.

I remember the Rill referred to by the member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie), which came before the committee last year. Some men from Vancouver-apparently in good standing, so far as the committee knew-had applied some years ago for a charter to- do an insurance-business. The charter was renewed once,, and they came back for another renewal last year. It was brought out at that time that the company had secured $70,000 or $72,000 in subscriptions and has squandered $63,000 or $64,000 of that in commissions. They were insisting on having the charter renewed in order that they could prosecute some of the stockholders for certain amounts which the company claimed were due them. That application was thrown out of committee. No evidence has been furnished this morning to satisfy this committee that the Bill now under consideration should be passed this year, in the dying days of the session. No- doubt it has been applied for in the ordinary way, but I do not see why the promoters could not have had their names in long before this. Now, in the dying days of the session, it is asked that this Bill be put through. I do not think we should stand for it; I think it should be laid over.

I observe that an hon. gentleman from Vancouver (Mr. Crowe) has entered the chamber. Perhaps he can give us- some light on the status of these gentlemen. A Bill has been introduced in the dying days of the session; it is not yet even printed in French.
The promoters of this Bill are a firm of lawyers in Ottawa. At the last moment, we are. informed that a number of gentlemen in Vancouver, who had not time to send their names here by letter, telegraphed their names, being anxious that they should be put in as tlhe promoters of this Bill. The whole thing is irregular, and I am anxious to know the status of these gentlemen. Their names are: H. S. Durkee, P. F. Wright, J. Kendall, O. S. Wood and
A.	G. Creelman. Are these the men who are new supposed to be the promoters of the-Bill, but who had not time to mail their application t-o get it here so as to comply with the rules

I do not know anything about the Bill before the House, but I know several of these gentlemen, and I can vouch .for them. Mr. Creelman is a large contractor in Vancouver, a very wealthy man. Mr. Wood is a man of A1 standing. Mr. Durkee is in the jewellery business, but I do not know what standing he has. Mr. P. F. Wright is in the furniture business. I can vouch for three of these gentlemen;

the other two I cannot vouch for because I do not know them.

subtopic: THE TAKING OF THE SOLDIERS' VOTE AT LAST ELECTION-AMENDMENT BY W. OOPP.
speechtext:
The
question I propose to discuss has reference to the taking of the soldiers' votes during the last general election, iboth in Canada and overseas. Those of us who were in this House during the sessions of 1915 and 1917 will well remember the attention that was paid to the Act giving the soldiers in Canada and overseas the right to record their votes at any general election in the Dominion, whenever that might be held. In the year 1915 there was a strong probability that a general election might be brought on before another session, and the Act I have referred to was passed giving the soldiers the right and privilege of exercising the franchise. The election was not held that year, and in 1917 a new Act was passed, amending the Dominion Elections Act and giving the soldiers the right to vote for or against the Government and for or against different candidates. As I propose to refer to a number of instances bearing on the different sections of the Military Voters' Act of 1917,
I shall put a few sections of the Act on Hansard. Section 3 says:
(1)	Every military elector shall be qualified and entitled to vote at a general election.
(2)	If he can state the electoral district wherein he last continuously resided during at least four months of the twelve months immediately preceding his appointment, enlistment, enrolment or calling out on active service, or so particularly specify a place or places within an electoral district whereat during such period of time he so resided that such electoral district can therefore be ascertained, he shall be deemed an elector of the electoral district so stated or to be ascertained, and his vote shall be supplied thereto.
(3)	If he cannot state or so specify an electoral district or place wherein, he has so resided for the time and within the period mentioned in subsection two but can state an electoral district or so specify a place within Canada wherein he has at any other time resided, he shall be deemed an elector of the electoral district so stated or made ascertainable and his vote shall be applied thereto.
(4)	If he cannot, because of non-residence or otherwise, so state or specify, he shall be deemed an elector of, and his vote shall be applied to, such electoral district as he may indicate.

(5)	No person shall be entitled, because of anything in this Part contained, to vote more than once at any election.
Section 5 says:
(1)	Whenever the Secretary of State of Canada shall so direct, a sufficient supply of ballot-papers in the form A of the Schedule, and of envelopes for holding the same, with certificates in the form iB of the Schedule printed thereon, and of all such forms and instructions as are ordinarily supplied to returning officers, modified to conform to the provisions of this Part, shall be delivered, (a) by the Clerk of the drown in Chancery to the officer in command of any Canadian forces in Bermuda, or in any other place without Canada but in North America, and to such Presiding Officers as shall have been appointed to arrange for the holding of polls in Canada; and, (b) by the Assistant Clerk of the Crown in Chancery to such Presiding Officers as shall have been appointed' to arrange for the holding of polls in the United Kingdom or on the continent of Europe.
(2)	Such ballot-papers and envelopes shall be safely held by such officers in command, respectively, until receipt from the 'Clerk of the Crown in Chancery of notice of the appointment of Presiding Officers for the camps under such officers' command, whereupon they shall deliver such ballots and envelopes to such Presiding Officers in such quantities as may be necessary, and! return any surplus, with a statement in writing of the disposition of all thereof, showing names and quantities, to the General Returning Officer at Ottawa.
(3)	The printer shall, upon delivering the ballot papers to the Assistant Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, file in his hands an affidavit setting forth the description of the ballots as printed by him, the number of ballots supplied by him, and the fact that no other ballot papers have been supplied by him to any one else.
Section 9, in part, reads as follows:
(1) The manner of voting without Canada under this Part shall be as follows:

(a)	Voting shall be by ballot;
(b)	The ballot-paper shall be in the formA in the Schedule;
(c)	The voter shall answer under oath, before the Deputy Presiding Officer, the questions set forth in the certificate which is form B in the Schedule. Such certificate shall be endorsed on the envelopes referred to in section five of this Part;

Mr. A. B. OOPP (Westmorland) resuming; Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at one o'clock I had just placed before hon. members of this Houee the sections of the Military Voters' Act to which I purpose to refer particularly during my argument. We all remember that at the time of the passing of that Act it was unanimously agreed by

all the hon. members of this House that every effort should be made to give to the soldiers who were fighting for our country the opportunity of voting in the election that was about to be held. We all remember also that during the discussion that took place in committee hon. gentlemen on both sides carefully considered each cfause of the Bill, and it was unanimously agreed that every safeguard that could be framed should be thrown around the measure to prevent the possibility of any fraud occurring in connection with the taking of the soldiers' vote. I well recall, Sir, the feelings that I entertained during that discussion, when certain of my hon. friends who are to-day on the other side- particularly my hon. friend from the: county of Carleto-n, N.B. (Mr. Carvell), now the Minister of Public Works in the present Government-took a very active part in that discussion. I am bound to admit that, while I had a very high regard for the acute and ingenious legal mind of my hon. friend (Mr. 'Carvell) I was somewhat convinced that he was over apprehensive as to the frauds that would be attempted in connection with the taking of that vote. But, Sir, now that I am in possession of the facte, 1 am satisfied that my hon. friend instead of being too careful and over apprehensive, did not foresee one-tenth part of the frauds that actually could be committed in connection with polling the soldiers' vote. I shall not occupy the time of the House by quoting, on the present occasion, the remarks of my hon. friend and of other hon. gentlemen on the occasion referred to.
I would suggest, however, to those who want to get the facts of the matter, and who now do me the honour of listening to my remarks, that if they will turn to the Revised Hansard of 1917, pages 4796 to 4870, they will learn what was in the minds of ho<n. gentlemen when the Military Voters' Act was being discussed in this House in Committee of the Whole.
After the Bill in question had been passed through committee and moulded into law the soldiers' vote was duly taken in this country, as well as overseas, and allocated, and, Sir, quite a large number of hon. members of the House now occupy their seats by virtue of the soldiers' votes cast on that occasion. For that reason it is only fair to ask the House to listen to some facts which I propose to lay before it as reasons why an inquiry should be instituted, and investigation made into the circumstances under which the soldiers' vote was taken, and that the results of that in-
[Mr. Copp.l
vestigation should be placed before the country. While the vote was being polled in Canada it came to my knowledge that irregularities were occurring. Shortly afterwards, and after the soldiers' vote had been taken overseas, I received numerous letters from soldiers who furnished me with information which convinced me that frauds, irregularities and election crimes had been committed. On the receipt of that information I deemed it to Ibe my duty to make further inquiries and endeavour to learn, as nearly as I could, the nature of those frauds. I started my inquiries and have received information, affidavits and statements, of the truth of which I have not the slightest doubt, and which convinces me that such irregularities were, practised in connection with the taking of the soldiers' vote in Canada and overseas. 1 therefore venture to- take up the time of the House this afternoon in order to place before Parliament and the people of the country the nature of those irregularities and frauds which, to my mind, prove beyond perad-venture that a conspiracy existed in connection with the allocation of those votes with the object of destroying the effect of the elections that were being held. Accordingly I have prepared some charges which I now propose to present to the House in proof of my contention that grievous irregularities and frauds were committed.
From information which I have received I have reason to believe, and do believe on my honour as a member of Parliament:
1.	That in the recent election a carefully organized conspiracy existed by which extensive frauds were perpetrated in connection with the soldiers' votes.
2.	That the aforesaid fraudulent conspiracy was particularly operative in the electoral districts of Kings and Queens, Prince Edward Island; Cape Breton North and Victoria, Richmond and Cape Breton South, Cumberland, Digby, Annapolis and Pdotou, Nova Scotia; Westmorland, Restigouche and Madawaska, Kent and Northumberland, New Brunswick; Brome, Sherbrooke, Chambiy-Vercheres, St. Ann's, Montreal, St. Antoine, St. Henri, St. Lawrence and St. George, Stanstead and Wright, Quebec; Algoma East, Bruce North and South, Essex North and South, Hamilton East and West, Huron South, Kent, Leeds and Brock-ville, Lennox and Addington, London, Middlesex West, Nipissing, Ontario South, Ottawa, Oxford South, Peel, Prince Edward, Russell, and Welland, Ontario ; Calgary, Edmonton, and the Yukon.

If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Currie) wishes to put a question I shall answer it to the best of my ability. I am trying to give the facts to the House clearly and honestly, feeling that it is my duty to do so. I shall discuss later the aspect of the question referred to by my hon. friend. Lieutenant-Colonel. Glenn, the deputy presiding officer, had this signed list before him when the vote was taken and must have known that the votes of the persons

to whom I have referred were placed in -a constituency in which they had no right to be placed.
I want to show the extent to which deputy presiding officers in England ignored the Act and permitted envelopes containing soldiers' votes to be placed in the ballot boxes with several of the answers required by the law not given.
Lieutenant R. R. H. Beaton, deputy presiding officer, Sunningdale, Ontario, permitted 133 envelopes, with questions 6, 7 and 8 not answered-one envelope only gave an answer to question 6-to be alloted to Prince Edward county, Ontario.
Lieutenant-Colonel G. G. Corbett, deputy presiding officer, permitted 274 envelopes to be placed in his ballot box for various constituencies in Ontario., out of which 174 did not answer questions 6, 7 and 8.
Major Cecil M. Roberts, deputy presiding officer, Bramshott camp, England, voted 609 envelopes. With the exception of 36, the entire poll was marked "cannot state" in reply to question 6. These votes were allocated to the constituencies of Essex, Bruce, Middlesex and Nipissing.
Lieutenant J. T. Allen, deputy presiding officer, permitted 237 votes to be polled for Ontario, out of which approximately 160 did not reply to questions 6, 7 and 8.
Captain H. J. Dennis, deputy presiding officer, polled a total of 808 votes, out of which 513 did not reply to questions 6, 7 and 8.
Out of a total of 589 envelopes placed in the ballot box of Major A. P. Gillis, deputy presiding officer, in only 314 were answers given to questions 6, 7 and 8.
Lieutenant-Colonel Malone, deputy presiding officer, 208th Battalion, polled a total of 766 envelopes, out of which 541 did not have answers given to questions 6, 7 and 8.
Under the supervision of Lieutenant J. R. Hayden, deputy presiding officer, 1,240 envelopes were polled at the regimental depot, practically all of which represented English-speaking soldiers. Out of this number, 1,200 did not answer questions 6, 7 .and 8.	999 of these envelopes were
placed in Quebec constituencies.

individual or isolated case that those frauds were committed, but that they were committed in practically every camp in which [DOT]the votes of soldiers were taken. Deputy presiding officers, if my information is correct and I have no doubt of its correctness, -committed frauds and conspiracies simply to defeat the will of the people of the Dominion of Canada in the election held on the 17th of December, 1917.
I want to refer to the statement I made in regard to Charge No. 7. To prove that charge, I am going to read to the House some affidavits which I hold in my hand. The first is an affidavit made by Louis Edmund Guillet:
1,	Louis Edmund Guillet a captain in the 150th Canadian Infantry Battalion of the fifth division of the Canadian Expeditionary Forces do hereby solemnly and sincerely declare as follows:-
1.	I was duly appointed in writing Deputy Scrutineer by William Thomas Rochester Preston under and for the purposes of the Military Voters' Act '1917.
2.	At or about 11.30 a.m. on Monday the 3rd day of December, 1917, I attended at the polling booth at Witley Camp at which polling booth the military electors comprised in the 125th Canadian Infantry Battalion were to register their votes for the pending Canadian election. I attended in my capacity as deputy scrutineer and I duly presented to the deputy presiding officer the document appointing me deputy scrutineer.
3.	Prior to the military electors entering the said polling booth for the purpose of voting they had already received from some person in some place other than the polling booth the envelopes with the questions printed thereon known as form B of the Military Voters' Act, 1917, and in nearly every instance the answers to the said questions in the said envelopes- had been filled in when they entered the said polling booth to vote.
4.	The military electors handed the envelopes so filled up and signed, to the deputy presiding officer who administered the oath and took the vote. I called the attention of the deputy presiding officer to the fact of the envelopes being filled in before the voter entered the polling booth and I asked the deputy returning officer where the answers were being written out and signed and he replied "in the company's offices". He also stated to me that after reading over the Act he considered this way of proceeding to take the vote to be the correct one.
5.	On the same day, Monday the 3rd December, 1917, I attended at the polling booth at Witley Camp at which polling booth the military electors comprised in the 156th Canadian Infantry Battalion were to register their votes for the same election. The same proceeding was being carried on at this polling booth namely, the military electors entered the said polling booth with envelopes already filled in outside the said polling booth, the oath was administered and the votes taken. I saw amongst others Lieut. Mason of the 156th Battalion attached to the 14th Canadian Infantry Brigade enter the polling booth with the answers to*the printed questions on his envelope already filled in outside the said polling booth.

6.	On the same day, 3rd December, 1917, I attended as deputy scrutineer at the polling booth at Witley Camp at which polling booth the military electors comprised in the 14th, 15th and 16th Canadian field ambulance sections were to register their votes for the said election, I saw several military electors enter the said polling booth with the answers to the questions on their envelopes already filled in and this had been done in another room and not in the said polling booth, I pointed out to the deputy presiding officer the voces were being taken not in compliance with the Act of Parliament and objected to his acting in this manner. The deputy presiding officer then called in two clerks who then proceeded to write out the answers of the military electors on their envelopes. The deputy presiding officer then asked the military electors the questions and read out the written answers himself.
7.	On the same day 3rd December, 1917, at about 3 p.m. I attended as deputy scrutineer at Witley Camp at which polling booth the military electors comprised the 208th .Canadian Infantry Battalion were to register their votes for the said election. I remained until 3.30 p.m. when the polling booth was closed. During this period about twenty military electors recorded their votes, they all brought into the said polling booth their envelopes with the answers to the printed questions thereon filled in outside the said polling booth and the deputy presiding officer in each case administered the oath and recorded the votes.
8.	On the following day the 4th December, 1917, I again as deputy scrutineer attended the last-mentioned polling booth and the military electors were voting in the way described in the preceding paragraph hereof. I then asked the deputy presiding officer to put the following questions to each military elector, "Were you in Canada when you enlisted" and "How long have you lived there" but the deputy presiding officer refused to put the questions to the said military electors who afterwards came in to record their votes.
9.	On the morning of Monday, the 3rd December, 1917, I attended at the polling booth at Witley Camp at which polling booth the military electors comprised in the 160th Canadian Infantry Battalion were to register their votes for the said election. I attended as deputy scrutineer and produced the document appointing me deputy scrutineer. No voting took place during the forenoon of that day. I attended at the same polling booth on the 4fh December, 1917, when voting was being carried on in the following manner. Each military elector was handed his envelope with the printed questions thereon which he took out of the said polling booth and filled in the answers in an adjoining room or office and he then returned to the said polling booth when the deputy presiding officer administered the oath and recorded his vote. Shortly before 1.30 p.m. on Tuesday, the 4th of December, 1917, accompanied by the said William Thomas Rochester Preston, I again attended at the said polling booth. I identified the said William Thomas Rochester Preston to the said Lt.-Col. W. P. Malone as the person appointed as scrutineer by Sir Wilfrid Laurier and the Canadian Opposition but the said Lt.-Col. W. P. Malone denied the right of the said William Thomas Rochester Preston to remain in the said polling booth during the polling and ordered the said William Thomas Rochester Preston to leave the said polling booth which

the said William Thomas Rochester Preston refused to do and thereupon the said Lt.-Cof. W. P. Malone called into the said polling booth the sergeant of the special guard and ordered the sergeant to bring- in the guard and remove the said William Thomas Rochester Preston from the said polling booth and thereupon the said sergeant requested the said William Thomas Rochester Preston to leave the said polling booth which the said William Thomas Rochester Preston refused to do and thereupon the said Lt.-Col. W. P. Malone ordered the said sergeant to take the said William Thomas Rochester Preston to the guard house which he accordingly did assisted by the guard.
And I make this solemn declaration conscientiously believing the same to be true and by virtue of the provisions of the Statutory Declarations Act, 1835.
(Sgd) Louis Edmund Guillet.
Declared at Witley Camp in the county of Surrey this 17th day of December, 1917, Before me,
Mr. Arthur Heywood,
A Commissioner for Oaths, etc., for use in Province of Ontario.

I accordingly entered the polling booth and announced to the Deputy Presiding Officer, Lieut.-Col. Graham, that I attended in my capacity as deputy scrutineer for the Opposition and I immediately directed his attention to the improper procedure then In vogue at that polling sub-division whereby the envelopes being part of the ballots were being improperly completed out of his possession and in the possession of persons outside the polling booth who were filling in the answers to the questions for Military electors who proposed voting thereon.
While I was present in the said polling booth one voter who had entered with his envelope duly filled up as hereinbefore stated was in the act of voting when I protested that the statements contained in the envelope must be filled in in the presence of the Presiding Officer and the scrutineer who was present for the purpose of learning and knowing what statements were being sworn to. The Presiding Officer informed me that this was unnecessary and voters were being sworn that the statements contained in the envelope were correct. I then requested



the scrutineers for the Opposition to make a note- of ail such votes recorded under these conditions and to enter a protest in each and every case, and demanded from the Presiding Officer that he note the protest of the official scrutineer for the Opposition.
I afterwards proceeded to the headquarters of the camp to interview the General Officer Commanding, Brigadier-General Hughes, who was not present. I therefore informed Colonel Parson who was acting on his behalf, and protested against this violation of the law which I had witnessed at said polling booth of the 156th Battalion. I also called upon the General Officer Commanding, General Meighan, of the Bramshott Camp, and informed him of what I had Witnessed at the Whitley Camp. He at once issued an order that no such procedure would be permitted within his district and each Deputy Returning Officer was notified accordingly. I immediately communicated with the said William Thomas Rochester Preston the facts concerned with this improper procedure at this polling sub-division as well as others within the Whitley Camp area.
And I make this solemn declaration conscientiously believing the same to be correct and by virtue of the provisions of the Statutory Declarations Act, 1835.
Declared at Westminster in the County of Middlesex this 22nd day of December, 1917.
(Sgd) T. D. Maefarlane.
Before me
(Sgd) W. T. R. Preston,
A Commissioner for Oaths for use in the Courts of the Province of Ontario.

I, Hugh Patrick McKinnon, a Quarter-Master-Sergeant in the 185th Canadian Infantry Battalion of the 5th Division of the Canadian Expeditionary Forces do hereby solemnly and sincerely declare as follows:
1. I was duly appointed in writing a Deputy Scrutineer to the 156th Canadian Infantry Bat-

talion by William Thomas Rochester Preston under and for the purposes of the Military Voters Act, 1917.

On Monday the 3rd December, 1917, I attended the polling booth at Witley Camp at which polling booth the military electors comprised in the 156th Canadian Infantry Battalion were to register their votes for the pending Canadian election. The reason given to me by the

Mr. Speaker, I have placed these affidavits before the House for the purpose of showing that these cases were not a few individual and isolated ones, and to demonstrate the manner in which the taking of the soldiers' vote was conducted in the Mother Country-those soldiers whom we spent our time here pledging ourselves to protect, and that advantage was taken by officials appointed by somebody- whoever was responsible for that electionr- to commit these wrongdoings. I have brought this matter to the attention of the House for its consideration, and I feel that the time occupied in doing so is amply justified when I present such facts as these.
Now I wish to refer to clause 8 of the charges alleging
That Opposition scrutineers were prevented from attending certain polling booths while the military vote was being allocated.
That has 'been covered in part by the affidavit of Mr. Guillet which I have already read, and also in the last clauee of Mr. Carmichael's declaration which I have just finished reading:
I want tQ place before the House another affidavit dealing with the charge that the scrutineer of the Liberal party was forced out of a polling booth and the vote taken in said military polling booth without any representative of the Opposition being there, as provided by the Military Voters Act:
In the matter of the Dominion Election Act as amended and affected by the War Time Election Act, 1917, and the Military Voters Act, 1917.
And in the matter of the election (1917) for the House of Commons of the Dominion of Canada.
And in the matter of the military voters for the purposes of the above election.
I, William Thomas Rochester Preston of "Kempshott", London Road, Norbury, in the county of Surrey, England, do solemnly and sincerely declare as follows :-
1. Pursuant to the Military Voters Act 1917 I was appointed scrutineer for and on behalf of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and the Canadian Opposition in respect of the military voting to take place in the United Kingdom of Great Britain
152$
for the pending election of members to the House of Commons for the Dominion of Canada, and I have duly complied with all the provisions of the said Act appertaining to a scrutineer.
2.	Notice of my said appointment was duly published in the General Military Orders issued by General Turner, commanding the Canadian Expeditionary Forces in London, and as scrutineer I have visited the polling booths at Witley Camp on several occasions with the approval of the commandant of the said Fifth Division, Brigadier General Hughes.
3.	Pursuant to the power vested in me under the said Military Voters Act, 19)17, I duly appointed (inter alia) the following persons as deputy scrutineers:
(a)	Sergeant Patenaude of the 150th Canadian Infantry Battalion.
(b)	Lance-Corporal D. S. Carmichael, of the 1'8'5th Canadian Infantry Battalion.
(c)	Q-Master H. L. McKinnon, of the 185th Canadian Infantry Battalion.
(d)	Corporal M. D. Kennedy, of the 185th Canadian Infantry Battalion.
(e)	Corporal W. C. Brennan, of the 185th Canadian Infantry Battalion.
(f)	Q-Master M. E. Falkner, of the 185th Canadian Infantry Battalion.
(g)	Captain L. E. Guillet, of the 150th Canadian Infantry Battalion.
(h)	Sergeant McCoy, of the 185th Canadian Infantry Battalion.
4.	From each of the said deputy scrutineers I received from time to time complaints of illegalities sanctioned and _ committed by the Deputy Presiding Officer at the polling booths at which they respectively attended in their capacity as scrutineers. At my request the said Deputy Scrutineers have made legal declarations of some of the said illegalities.
5.	In addition to the illegalities referred to in the preceding paragraph many more illegalities of a similar nature have occurred legal evidence as to which is now in process of being collected.
6.	As an illustration of the high handed illegal treatment to which I and some of the Deputy Scrutineers appointed by me have been subjected by certain of the Deputy Returning Officers, I desire to record the following facts:-
On Tuesday morning the 4th December 1917 I attended the said Polling Booth at Witley Camp wherein the Military Electors of the 208th Canadian Infantry Battalion were recording their votes. I had previously been informed that on Monday the 3rd December 1917 the day preceding my regularly appointed Scrutineer Captain Guillet in the said polling booth had been refused permission to remain during the voting. I produced letters from Lieutenant Colonel Purney the deputy of the clerk of the Crown in Chancery establishing my identity to the Deputy Presiding Officer Lieutenant Colonel W. P. Malone but he refused to acknowledge my right to be present and ordered me to withdraw from the said polling booth and on my refusing to comply with his directions he declared the poll to be closed.
7.	Having ascertained that the said poll was to be reopened in the said polling booth at the hour of 1.30 p.m. on the said 4th December 1917 I returned to the said polling booth accompanied by Captain Guillet of the 150th Canadian Infantry Battalion of the 5th Division of the Canadian Expeditionary Forces one of the Deputy Scrutineers appointed by me as aforesaid and he in my presence and in the

presence of the said Deputy Presiding Officer the said Lieutenant Colonel W. P. Malone identified me to the said Lieutenant Colonel W. P. Malone as Mr. W. T. R. Preston the Scrutineer appointed by the said Sir Wilfrid Laurier and the Canadian Opposition under the said Military Voters Act 19T7. The said Captain Guillet had previously complained to me that he had been prevented from remaining at the said polling Booth by the said Deputy Presiding Officer Lieutenant Colonel W. P. Malone. Notwithstanding the production by me of the said letter from Lieutenant Colonel Purney and the identification of me by the said Captain Guillet the said Deputy Presiding Officer. Lieutenant Colonel W. P. Malone denied my right to remain in the said polling booth during the polling therein and ordered me to leave the said polling booth which X refused to do, and thereupon the said Deputy Presiding Officer the said Lieutenant Colonel W. P. Malone called in to the said polling booth a sergeant of the special guard which was in attendance and ordered the said sergeant to bring in the guard and remove me from the said polling booth. The said Sergeant then requested me to leave the said polling booth which I refused to do and thereupon the said Deputy Presiding Officer the said Lieutenant Colonel W. P. Malone addressing the said Sergeant said "Remove this man and take him to the Guard House". Accordingly the Sergeant seized me forcibly and removed me from the said polling booth and accompanied by the said Sergeant the said guard with fixed bayonets conducted me to the Guard House and placed me In an inner room used as a detention cell where there were incarcerated a number of soldiers, charged with military offences. I was detained in the said Guard House for a period of about two and a half hours when, escorted by a guard under command of an officer I was marched to General Headquarters a distance of about one mile where I was received in the first instance by Major Green and who was astonished to hear of the treatment to which I had been subjected. At my request in confirmation of the facts heretofore declared to by me as to my arrest I received through the said Major Green a memorandum in the following terms:
"To the 13th Canadian Inf. Batt.
4,	XII, 1917.
"Mr. W. T. R. Preston who has been officially appointed a Scrutineer in connection with the Dominion Elections (Vide D.O.C.R.O. 2842) has permission to enter polling booths within this Camp area.
(Signed) Major Green,
D. A. A. & Q.M.G.
5th Canadian Division.
And I make this solemn declaration conscientiously believing the same to be true and by virtue of the provisions of the Statutory Declarations in this behalf.
(Signed) W. T. R. Preston.
Declared before me at Ottawa in the County of Carleton this 21st day of May, 1918.
(Signed) D. C. Ross,
A Commissioner for Oaths.
Mr. Speaker, that affidavit, together with that part of the affidavits of Mr. Guillet and Mr. Carmichael that deals with this
[Mr. Copp.j
particular matter, proves beyond question paragraph 8 as set forth in the charges.
The next charge, No. 10, refers to the questions on the envelopes toeing partially filled in and signed and sealed toy the deputy presiding officer, and each containing a ballot marked for the Government toeing in circulation for the perpetration of the charges hereinbefore mentioned. I hold in my hand an envelope, under Form B, signed toy Lieutenant W. G. Bryan, deputy presiding officer. This envelope is an exact copy of an envelope that was found during the counting and allocating of the soldiers' votes in 'England. The Iballot within was initialled and the envelope, with several of the questions answered, was signed by the deputy returning officer, tout the name of the soldier voter was left blank.
I now wish to read an affidavit made by W. D. Spence, in regard to this:
In the matter of the Elections for the House of Commons of the Dominion of Canada holden in the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, December lst-17,	1917, under the
provisions of the Military Voters Act, A.D. 1917.
I, William David Spence, of the City of Calgary, in the Province of Alberta, Canada, accountant and Special Returning Officer in the matter herewith, make oath and say:
That in my capacity as Special Returning Officer I received from ballot box 152 an envelope sealed with the following endorsements thereon, the answers being to questions (2) "Pte.".... (3) "21st Alberta Reserve" (4) "Yes" and second part of question 4 "No". "Dated this 10th day of December 1917, (Sd.) W. C. Bryan, Lieut.-Deputy Presiding Officer."
Upon opening the envelope I found a ballot therein marked in compartment (2) "I vote for the Government" with a cross heavily marked in lead pencil.	,
I make this Affidavit on my soul conscien- , tiously believing the statements herein to be true by virtue and under the provisions of Act of Parliament passed for this purpose A.D. 1835.
W. D. Spence.
Sworn before me in the city of Westminster, in the county of Middlesex, England, this sixth day of March, A.D. 1918.
(Sd.) W. T. R. Preston, Commissioner for taking oaths,
&c., &c., &c.
That goes to prove, Mr. Speaker, that there was an effort made, and not only made, hut carried into effect, that envelopes were taken and filled in and signed by a returning officer with the name of the elector left blank and the ballot placed ins'de the envelope marked " for the Government " for the purpose of finding the name of some elector that could be written in at the last moment, and the envelope placed in the ballet box. This is another irregularity,

another fraud, in the conspiracy to defeat the will of the Canadian people in the elections.
Mr. Speaker, the next charge (No. 11) is:
That military electors were canvassed by superior officers in direct contravention of the King's regulations and orders, and were directed how they should mark their ballots.
I have here a statement-not' an affidavit or declaration-made by a gentleman who has already given an affidavit, Mr. T. D. Macfarlane, one of the scrutineers for the Opposition in that election. It reads-
As your representative in the United Kingdom as scrutineer, I beg to report conditions as I found them through the northern pa. t of England at hospitals where Canadian votes were taken, also at Canadian hospitals and other centres.
At the first southern General Hospital, Birmingham, in charge of Capt. J. M. Suttie, Deputy Presenting Officer for the Union Government, I found votes were taken in the various wards, envelopes filled and prepared for the voter in the presence of other voters and instructions given to the voter where to mark his cross, indicating the space opposite Union Government. This applies also to the 21st Southern General Hospital, the First Birmingham War Hospital and the 2nd Birmingham War Hospital under the direction of Lieut. C. E. Haywood, presiding officer.
I next visited the Canadian Discharge Depot, Buxton, presiding officers-Lieut-Colonel A. R. Hanson, Capt. A. Maclean, Lieut. F. W. Lock, Capt. A. D. Gordon, Lieut. C. E. Field.

subtopic: THE TAKING OF THE SOLDIERS' VOTE AT LAST ELECTION-AMENDMENT BY W. OOPP.
speechtext:
I interviewed a number of. the soldiers at the depot and from all I learned that a general canvass had been made with a view of arranging voting and the placing of districts in which votes would be applied; among the number canvassed was a young man of 19 who gave me his name as Malcolm, of Vancouver, who joined the Artillery at Victoria, B.C. He mistook me for a representative of the Union Government and gave me the following information :	That all of them were supporting the
Union Government, and that a large number of them had arranged that their votes would be applied in whatever constituency they were required at the last moment and said they were to be applied in Quebec, but the district would not be selected until they knew where these
votes were needed in order to defeat an Opposition candidate.
I also interviewed a soldier in the Canadian army who said that when in Canada he lived at Oxbow and Alameda, Saskatchewan, but left there in 1906 and lived in America until he joined the Army and that he was requested to name Wentworth as the district in which his vote would be recorded.
At the Crescent Hotel, Buxton, where I was stopping, the proprietor and a guest were discussing the Canadian Election Act. I was brought into the conversation by a reference from the guest who inquired of me if elections were conducted in Canada on the same lines as they were carried on here. These men stated that the arrangement enabled the soldier from any part of Canada to register his vote where desired by the Presiding Officer, when I replied that the voter was only entitled to a vote for the candidate in the district in which he had lived. In answer to this guest informed me that he had discussed the matter with officers in charge of the voting; this was verified by the proprietor of the hotel in which they said that officers of the Canadian army informed them that by this method they were going to defeat any candidate they chose, and the whole subject appeared to be a huge joke to the officers discussing it. It appeared to be common knowledge of residents who came in contact with officers or other members of the Canadian army.
I also visited the two Canadian hospitals at Buxton and in conversation with voters I learned that the general arrangements of conducting the vote for the Union Government were so pronounced that those desiring to vote otherwise could not do so fearing detection and disapproval of the Staff generally. At most of the Canadian hospitals and other places conducted by the Canadian officials there was an absence of the necessary list of candidates posted; but in nearly every case there was the usual literature for campaign purposes posted on the gates and on the building-one of these posters stating that ''Germany was praying for the defeat of the Union Government-Vote for the Union Government and furnish recruits to relieve our men at the front".
I visited two British hospitals in Manchester . where Canadian soldiers voted. A similar condition to the Birmingham hospital was carried on there.
I also visited a number of Canadian Lumber Camps in Inverness district, including 107, 110, and 121. The polling had taken place in a.11 these camps before I reached there, but in conversation with various soldiers a general impression in almost every case was the necessity of supporting the Government by which they were employed.
From the Canadian Camps I went to Aberdeen and there visited the Old Mill Hospital which only contained a very small number of Cana-, dians. One Canadian, by the name of Emery, stated that there was no choice of candidates as the Deputy Presiding Officer informed him in which space to make his cross

opposite the Union Government. I also visited the 1st Scottish General Hospital, Aberdeen, and found pretty much the same conditions.
I then visited the 1st Scottish General Hospital in Edinburg. Polling had been completed and the information regarding the conduct of the voting was on the same lines as the other hospitals. This also applies to the 3rd and 4th Scottish General Hospitals of Glasgow.

ing booths where the soldiers' votes were being taken.
