subtopic: THE TAKING OF THE SOLDIERS' VOTE AT LAST ELECTION-AMENDMENT BY W. OOPP.
speechtext:
I am not discussing the high standing of the gentleman. I am not here to discuss or tO' debate, or to say -an ill word of any individual; I am placing before the House the facts as I have them; and if Lieut.-Col. Thompson-I care not how high his record is, nor how long he sat in this House-took part in a conspiracy to defeat the will of the people of this country, he is not worthy of being sent to represent the Government in looking after the taking of the votes of the soldiers overseas. I have no doubt of the truth of the evidence which I have under my hand, and it is true, that Lieut.-Col. Thompson, under the Military Voters' Act, under which authority he was acting at that time, had no authority an-d no right to appoint scrutineers to represent the Liberal party, it was beneath the dignity of any honourable citizen, to thus appoint a representative to act on behalf of the Opposition party led by my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), particularly when- Lieut.-Col. Thompson was overseas representing the Government party to which my right hon. friend was opposed.
The appointment of another deputy scrutineer reads:
By virtue of the powers vested in me by the Military Voters' Act, 1917, I hereby appoint Harry Stevens, corporal, as my deputy.
(sgd) A. T. Thompson, Lt.-Col. Scrutineer. Let me see what the oath says:
Oath to be taken by deputy scrutineer or military elector representing party.
I, the undersigned, Harry Stevens, Corpora], a deputy scrutineer or military elector (as the case may be) under the Military Voters' Act, 1917, representing the Opposition party, do swear that I will keep secret the votes cast by -any of the voters at the polling stations at which I acted as such representative.
Sworn before me at Buxton, Derbyshire, this 29th day of November, 1917.
('Sgd.) Philip Burnett,
Deputy Presiding Officer.
This is a soldier who was appointed by Lt.-Col. Thompson, who represented the Government . That was another case where Lt.-Col Thompson appointed -a scrutineer who was afterwards sworn in 'as scutineer for the Opposition. I am not here to eiay what was Lt.-Col. Thompson's intention when in these appointments he appoints two scrutineers, one sworn :n as representing the Opposition party and the other sworn in as representing the Government party. I am here to place that fact before the House, and I appeal to every hon. member here who wants to he straightforward and honest in winning an election: Would he feel'that he was doing the right thing if he went into hie opponent's constituency and appointed a scrutineer to act for his opponent and look after his interests during an election campaign or during the polling of the votes in that particular constituency on election day? That is not his prerogative; that is not his right, and I cannot come to any other conclusion than that any gentleman who takes such a course is abusing his right and privilege for the purpose of endeavouring to make it appear to the presiding officer that the Opposition party, as well as the Government party, was feeing represented when, as a matter of fact, only one party was being represented, and that was fey men who were appointed and sworn in by and at the instigation and request of Lt.-Col. A. T. Thompson, who was representing the Government and not the Opposition.
I come next to charge No. 16:
That election campaign literature which was dishonest and untruthful was circulated among the military electors with the authority and by the direction of Lord Beaverbrook, and that the said Lord Beaverbrook was an active participant in the hereinbefore mentioned fraudulent practices.
We have already heard in this House during this session a statement by the leader of the Opposition, speaking on the Address, when he referred to the taking of' the soldiers' votes and the literature connected therewith and exhibited to this House a photograph that had been taken of a polling booth on which were election posters directing the electors how they should cast their votes. As that phase of the case will be taken up by some other hon. members who will follow me, I shall not take up the time of the House in referring to it, as that would only mean repetition. I am not going to discuss that phase of the question any -more than to say tha't the information I have and the literature I have seen convince -me beyond a

doubt that that statement is Absolutely correct.
In reference to the next charge, No. 17:
That Lord Brooke, formerly Commander of the Canadian Forces, was also a participant in the said fraudulent practices.
I have not personal knowledge as to Lord Brooke's domicile before he went overseas during this war; I only have the information from friends. I understand that Lord Brooke was a resident of and domiciled in Calgary, Alberta; but I find from a record that Lord Brooke, a gentleman whom I do not know but who, from his name, I would judge is a man of some substance and *standing-he received his title anyway before this matter came up in discussion yesterday-did not vote in the constituency in which I am informed he lived, but he voted in Provencher, in the province of Manitoba, a constituency in which he had no legal qualification to vote. I only give the House the information I have. I do not personally know what his domicile was; but if he was domiciled in Calgary before he went overseas, he had no right under the Military Voters' Act to select a constituency in the province of Manitoba wherein to cast his vote, and if he did so, that must have been for one purpose, namely, because he thought his vote in that particular constituency in the province of Manitoba would be of more benefit to the Government party than his vote in the city of Calgary.

speechtext: On what authority does my hon. friend say that Lord Brooke was located at Calgary?

subtopic: THE TAKING OF THE SOLDIERS' VOTE AT LAST ELECTION-AMENDMENT BY W. OOPP.
speechtext:
I do not say anything of the kind. I said I had been told by a number of persons that Lord Brooke's domicile was in the city of Calgary, and I therefore contend that he had no right under the Military Voters' Act to cast his vote in the constituency of Provencher, in the province of Manitoba.
The next charge is ae followc:
That letters mailed through the Canadian Army Branch of the British Post Office, addressed to military electors, in which was enclosed campaign literature on behalf of the Opposition, were opened, and the said literature was removed therefrom before the said letters were delivered to the military electors, to whom they were addressed, and the delivery of the said letters was also systematically delayed by the said post office authorities.
The evidence I have on that point is that envolopes containing letters and literature were mailed in the city of London to the soldiers who were in the different camps there and also in France. These letters were returned after the election, some of them marked "Unknown" and others marked in different ways. But strange to say, the envelopes had been opened and the literature extracted and then the envelope sealed up again. If the post office system in London is anything similar to the Canadian system, an odd letter might go astray, but surely it is not chance when such a large number of letters, all mailed to people of the same class, should be returned. But that is the information I have, and if it is true, it is but another link in the chain of conspiracy prevailing at the time the soldiers votes were being taken. I wrote a number of letters myself in the month of November last to military electors from my constituency, and while I did not get replies from all, I got replies from a large number of soldiers, and almost without exception they said that they had not received the letters until two or three, and in some cases ten, days after the election.

opened Wednesday, January 9th, or Thursday, the 10th. Rolls of ballots containing two s, three's, four's or more, were found closely rolled together, too large to have been inserted through the opening on the top of the bag.
These bags were locked before opened by the officers, but whether or not there was any space within the chained opening through which papers might have been inserted, we are not prepared to state. There was not anything in the external appearance of any of the bags to lead us to believe that they had been opened.
Bag No. 153 was opened on Friday, January 11th. Bag was locked before opened by the election officers. Rolls were taken from it which were too large to have gone through the aperture on the top. These rolls consisted of ballots closely rolled together, of different dates, one roll' of ballots was dated December 7th and 10th, and another roll of six ballots had at least four different dates. We are not positive as to how tightly the opening of the bag was secured by the lock and chain.
Bag No. 155 opened on Monday morning, January 14th. Dock and chain examined before opened and found not tightly closed, and opening could bo made size of two fingers. Rolls of ballots taken therefrom in three's, four's, and sixes. These rolls could not have been inserted through the aperture on the top of the bag.
Bag No. 102, opened Monday morning, January 14th, Colonel Purney being present. Dock and chain were examined carefully before opened and found tight and closely locked, and a few ballots were taken therefrom. Rolls were found closely folded together, three, four, and more together in rolls, which could not have gone through the aperture on the ,top of the bag.
It is contended on the one hand that the opening which might be made in the neck of the bags through the chain being loosely locked, would allow the folded envelopes to be placed within the bag through such an opening, and on this account the suggestion that the boxes have been opened for an improper purpose, is not justified.
On the other hand, it is contended that as the envelopes which were folded together could not he inserted in the bags through the small flap covered aperture, the conclusion is justified that the said boxes come under the clause of the Act which declares that the^ contents of certain boxes shall not be examined, and

that therefore the ballots therein shall not be counted.

Mr. Speaker, 1 have placed before the House and the country the facts which I desired it my duty to make known. I can assure you, that I do not bring this matter before the House for any personal feeling I have in the matter, or any personal feeling I have against any hon. member in this House, nor do I so because the -overseas vote or the soldiers' vote in Canada made any difference in my election [DOT]or anything of that kind. This information, as I said at the beginning of my remarks, came to me from soldiers themselves in answer to letters that I had sent to them .-and that were not delivered until after the votes had been cast. They stated to me that the letters were not delivered until after the vote was taken. They gave me ,a number of illustrations of irregularities *and frauds that had been committed in the polling booths where the military electors went to cast their ballots under the Military "Voters' Act that was passed at the last .session of Parliament. Being prompted by those letters, I commenced to make some inquiries. I made those inquiries in the best possible way I could. I made investigations; I compared, where that was possible, the nominal Tolls of the *officers and men. I satisfied myself that gross irregularities took place in the taking of the soldiers' votes, and frauds and election crimes were committed in regard -io the taking of that vote. The opportunity afforded me of investigating matters was indeed meagre and, in a great measure, [Mr. Copp.j
I had to secure a good deal of information from hostile witnesses, but nevertheless I secured that information and I believe it to be true. When I pieced together the different portions of evidence that I had gathered, I was satisfied that gross irregularities and frauds toad been perpetrated in the taking of the soldiers' votes. I said at the outset that, when the Military Voters' Act was going through this House, it was stated that just such frauds and irregularities as these would be the result Those apprehensions were well grounded, and I think I have given absolutely convincing evidence that the irregularities that were feared have taken place. I have taken up a great deal of the time of the House in presenting this argument.
Some hon. MEMBER'S: Hear, hear.

I realized that this task
would be unpopular with hon. gentlemen opposite, but when one has a matter of this kind to bring before Parliament and the country one must make an argument such as he would make before a court of law, and it should be in sequence as far as possible. I have endeavoured to do that. I did not undertake this duty to gain the plaudits of hon. gentlemen around me, nor did I shirk it because it would be unpopular amongst hon. gentlemen opposite. I knew that the duty devolved upon me or some other member on this side of the House to bring the facte before the public.
I have undertaken that responsibility, and I leave it to the country to judge whether or not I have done my duty. Before taking my seat J beg to move:
That an investigation be held conducted by a judge of a court of superior jurisdiction, assisted by two counsel, one to be selected by the Brime Minister and the other by the leader of the Opposition, to examine into the taking

and counting of the military votes cast in the last general election, with power to order the production of all cables, telegrams, correspondence, toll books, nominal rolls of regiments and papers and documents of all kinds, and with power also to summon and examine witnesses, except soldiers whose attendance at the inquiry would interfere, in the opinion of the judge, with their military duties.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it would have been a pity if the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Copp) who states he has not shirked his duty-and I am quite sure this House will be confirmed in that view, if he conceived it to be his duty to make a speech of this kind, seeing that he has taken four hours to deliver it-it would have been a pity indeed if he had forgotten, the principal part of his speech, in which he desired to move for a committee of inquiry on a matter in respect of which, I submit, he has given no reason at all why a committee of inquiry should be appointed. However,
I do not want to dwell on that.
In the first place I would ask my hon. friend, who has brought this matter up at such great length, what on earth was the good of bringing it up, and stating what he has stated at this particular time? He has talked a great deal about fraud and crime. I am not sure that it is not a crime perpetrated against this House on the night before prorogation to take up four hours of the time of this House in trying to prove a case which he has not begun to prove. If there had been a situation where the mandate of the people, coupled with the mandate of those who are Canadian citizens across the seas, had been of so undecided a character that there was doubt in the minds of this nation whether or not this Government should be supported in its policies, I could quite understand that with the feeling of soreness, perhaps, that all people and all parties have wh'en they are defeated in an election they might bestir themselves and say, "Well, this is a very narrow margin; possibly something has been going on against the law; let us pursue the matter and see if we cannot turn the scales." But that was not the case here. The case here is that without a single soldier vote overseas or in Canada, this Union Government and its policies has been so absolutely and so substantially
endorsed that there has been no question as to a mandate from the people of Canada, and it is rather amusing to hear my hon. friend express his horror at the desperate things that have been going on, and the pain it has given him. Personally I did not see any great evidence of pain when the hon. member was bringing up this matter in the way he has. Throughout all his speech there is not only an admission that he attacks the political side of this thing-political in the sense that all politicians understand, namely, the methods and practices of those not holding office, but who are desirous, nevertheless, of returning their party to power-but there is also an implication or plain charge that the administration of this Election Act by the officials appointed for that purpose has been of a deplorable character. Before saying another word, I resent in the strongest possible way the imputations that have been cast by the hon. member on the character of the officers who have carried forward this election in Canada, in England, and in France, and I think the best answer I can give my hon. friend aEter his four hours' speech would be this: that he has not said, practically, a single word or made a single charge in regard to the administration of the Act and the running of the election in France or in Canada, but has confined practically all of his criticisms and charges to the conduct of the election in England. I would point out to this House what many members know, that there have been the same administration, the same rulings and decisions, and practically the very same methods, in France, in England, and in Canada. In France we have had no complaints; in Ca*nada we have had virtually no complaints. Indeed, my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) himself commended the way in which the general returning officer, Mr. O'Connor, had conducted election affairs in Canada. Mr. Langlois, the gentleman appointed by the right hon. leader of the Opposition to take chief charge in France, commended Colonel Purney, the Assistant Clerk of the Crown in Chancery overseas, for the way he had conducted affairs so far as France was concerned. My hon. friend attempts to show that things were conducted in a different way in England from that in which they were conducted in Canada or France. That charge is absolutely without foundation. Mr. O'Connor had charge of the administration of the Act and the conduct of the elections in Canada, and waa constantly in touch, every day, by cable
By whom was the ruling given to which my hon. friend has referred?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: That ruling was 'given by the general returning officer and by Colonel Purney, and was followed out.
My hon. friend is mistaken.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: No, I am absolutely right.

The general returning officer had nothing to do with giving the ruling. The Order in Council passed by my hon. friend and his colleagues calls upon the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery to give the ruling, not the general returning officer.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: A decision was given by the proper authority, and the Assistant Clerk of the Crown in Chancery overseas gave that ruling.

The general returning
officer had nothing to do with it. The clerk of the Crown in Chancery here gave the ruling and the assistant clerk of the Crown in Chancery overseas followed it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The ruling was given and absolutely followed, that is what 1 am contending for.
All right.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Therefore, the argument of my hon. friend, who seems to contend that all these votes where questions 6, 7 and 8 were not answered should not have been given, is absolutely beside the mark, because none of those ballots were ailo-cated at all. In fact, in England, out of
104,000	votes Which were cast, 17,000 ballots were rejected, and rejected largely because of that very reason. Indeed, I think there were a great many men who, perhaps, suffered an injustice by being done out of their votes. Furthermore, the candidates concerned, who did not receive the votes of those men, who honestly believed they were entitled to vote, were adversely affected. At all events, rightly or wrongly, that rigid interpretation of the law to which I have just referred was given, so that the number of men I -have mentioned were not permitted to vote, and in France there was about the same proportion. In Canada alone no less than 19,000 votes were rejected, and very largely for the reason I have indicated.
I would also like to point out another fallacy indulged in by my hon. friend and to indicate to him that the fulminations and the heat which he displayed, and the fiery indignation into which he worked himself on this point, were entirely wasted energy. He argued-and if he is sincere I can only say it shows great ignorance on his part of the actual facts of the case- that it was the deputy presiding officers who allocated all these votes in, as he says, this improper way. That is what I understand the hon. gentleman to argue-that the deputy presiding officer allocated these
TMr Burrell.]
votes although he should not have alio-cated them-thus implying grossly improper proceedings on the part of election officials in this matter. Now, as every member of the House knows-or many members do- the deputy presiding officers had absolutely nothing whatever to do with allocating the votes; they were simply there for the purpose of receiving the votes; and: the allocation was done by the Assistant Clerk of the Crown in Chancery in England; by Mr. O'Connor in Canada, and by the gentleman [DOT] appointed for the purpose in France. The allocation was carried out according to the merits and facts of the ease, and according to the law, and in the presence of two men, one of whom was appointed by the Union Government and the other by my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition. I cannot see where all the indignation manifested by my hon. friend enters at all on this subject; I think his whole ease falls to the ground.
Now let me deal with another charge that the hon. gentleman made. He spoke several times about improprieties in connection with the ballot envelopes. He argued that there were improper things going on because of military voters in England filling out their envelopes before they came to the polling places to vote, and that the whole thing was extremely irregular. He alleged that a lot of this occurred at Witley in particular, and also in connection with the 156th Battalion under Lieutenant Cblonel Grant. Well, that is true enough. It is not true that the ballots were filled out before the electors came to the polling place, but it is true that some were filled out before the men actually came into the polling room. As a matter of convenience some of them were filled out at Witley in an adjoining room, but, let me observe, undier the Presiding Officer and sworn to and attested by him. After all, I do not know that there is anything illegal about that. It is true,, it may not have been a literal or full compliance with the Act, and that it was afterwards discouraged 'by Colonel Purney, who stopped it; but after all, what does it amount to? The Act requires that the voters shall come to the Deputy Presiding Officer and answer certain questions that appears on the envelope as to whether they were resident in Canada, and so on. The voter was supposed to swear to those answers, and then the certificate was attested by the Presiding Officer. I would ask, however, what is the difference between a Deputy Presiding Officer giving

the voter an envelope and getting him to fill it in himself and then returning and handing it in and the Presiding Officer himself seeing that the envelope is filled out. What is the difference between putting the oath to the voter as to whether his answers are correct or not, and putting the oath to him before he filled out the envelope. The man gave his oath that those were his true answers, and I cannot see anything in that contention hut. a matter of hair-splitting. Although, it is true, it was not a strict compliance with the law it was only done for a short time, and done under proper supervision. Surely my hon. friend would not argue in any conceivable way that that was improper, or in any real sense an illegal proceeding? To say that that constituted evidence of a dark, dangerous, sinister conspiracy on the part of people unknown, I think would be a very far-fetched idea.
While on the envelope question my hon. friend waxed eloquent because envelopes bad been put in which had not been properly filled out, or filled out before the voter went to the poll. I think that is what my hon. friend argued, although I do not want to do him an injustice. He held up a white envelope at that time.
No, I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Very good. If my hon. friend held up an official envelope I have nothing to say. If he had held up a white envelope it would be perfectly natural because a large number of white envelopes were used by 'both parties for instructional purposes, many of which, through ignor-[DOT] ance or dishonesty, were put into the various polling bags, but were rejected and destroyed at the final count. I certainly thought that was one of these enveloDes.
Will my hon. friend say where these envelopes were used for instructional purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I think they were used in England and 'Canada and by both sides I am informed. My hon. friend in the course of his remarks animadverted on the case of United States citizens voting. Here he again seems to scent some evidence of a dark and deep-laid conspiracy to get them to do improper things. In the first place, no United States citizens, as he knows, can vote under the law, although here again it was industriously spread throughout my province that this Act was so intricate that it allowed United States citizens to vote in an election. I am sure everybody who
knows anything about it should know that no United States citizen could vote. It is true that if he filled'out in the answer to No. 5-(first of all he has to 6ay whether he is a British subject, and if he said he was, and answered No. 5:	"Were you in
Canada when you enlisted?" in the negative, then I maintain he was within the law in answering No. 9. I am not pronouncing on the question as to what would be done if a United States-citizen deliberately perjured himself by saying " yes " in answer to question No. 4, " Are you a British subject?" That is a different point altogether. The onus of that must rest on the individual. But as far as the election officers go, and as far as the administration of this Act goes, there is absolutely not a shadow of impropriety in regard to such a charge about United States citizens voting.
Now, I wish to come to another criticism which my hon. friend made, and that was in relation to Colonel A. T. Thompson, who is very well known and very much liked by a great many men on both sides of the House, and who formerly sat as a member of this1 House, and was a very strong and pronounced supported of my right hon friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) for years. 1 might say in this connection that the gentlemen who were appointed as chief scrutineers by my right hon. friend and by the Prime Minister, and who -are by implication aesailed through the speech of my hon. friend, were these:
In France, Major Gibson, representing the Government as chief scrutineer in the whole of the United Kingdom, Colonel A. T. Thompson; in Canada, Mr. John F. Orde, K.-C., rwho is well known here. The leader of the Opposition appointed in France Mr. God-froi Langlois, who is well known; in England, Mr. W. T. R. Preston, who is also well known; and in Canada, Mr. W. R. Hearn. I do not think that any man in this House would care to say what my hon. friend in his speech this afternoon said, that however high a standing Colonel Thompson may have had, he allowed this most deplorable conduct in the -selection, for that is the effect of his charges. He said that Colonel Thompson appointed two scrutineers, one for the Opposition and one for the Government, and thereby misled everybody, and worked in a Government man masquerading as an Opposition man and did a great injury -to- the party o? my hon. friends opposite. My hon. friend surely knows that Colonel Thompson, as chief scrutineer, does not appoint an Opposition scrutineer and assign him to a particular place, because the whole inference of my

hon. friend's remarks was that at a certain polling place Colonel Thompson had put in two men, one a Government man and one an Opposition man to work in a particular poll.

If I may be permitted: I said that Colonel Thompson appointed two scrutineers, and that the presiding officer swore one in as a scrutineer for the Opposition and the other as a scrutineer for the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend cannot get away from the fact that he impugned Colonel Thompson in that respect. Because, when he was interrupted by the hon. mernbeT for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) he got rather heated about it, and certainly left the impression in my mind, and in the minds of hon. gentlemen on this side, that Colonel Thompson had done something very dark. Colonel Thompson was the chief scrutineer for the whole of the United Kingdom and the Channel Islands, and, as anybody who has anything to do with elections knows, he had tb issue hundreds of certificates for the appointment of scrutineers, and he would issue them by the hundred. He would not always know where these certificates went. He might issue them with a name, and again it might possibly be left in blank. He does not appoint these scrutineers to go to a particular place. Here is an Opposition and a Government man. That man goes himself andi takes his oath before another officer as to whether he is an Opposition scrutineer or whether he is a Government scrutineer. And upon that man and upon that officer who takes that oath is the onus of saying whether that man is an Opposition or a Government man. It is quite conceivable, to one whose mind is not so full of dark suspicions as my hon. friend's, that in the issuance of hundreds of certificates to scrutineers, mistakes should occur. If I wanted to get highly suspicious, I might as well argue that one of these certificates was filled in by my hon. friends opposite for the purpose of saying that this was a cooked-up case. I do not want to assume such things. It is very much beside the mark that my hon. friend should draw the deduction from such a slender hypothesis as this that Colonel Thompson, as a Government officer, has been behaving in a highly improper way.
My hon. friend followed that by the remark that Mr. Preston, the chief scrutineer appointed by my right hon. friend who leads the Opposition, had been maltreated in England, bad not been dealt with

properly, and that he had even been arrested at one time. Well, I am afraid that Mr. Preston was arrested; I cannot deny that. As a matter of fact, what happened was this: Mr. Preston was the only civilian who was operating as an election officer of any kind practically, in Great Britain. They were all military men, and every one of them in uniform. And Mr. Preston appears at some military camp and states that he is Mr. Preston and is a scrutineer, and does not produce anything to show that he is. As I understand it, he had the papers on him, but would not produce them. And the military authorities, in times like these, when civilian gentlemen, whom nobody knows, assume that they are something, and take no steps to show that they- are, the military also, like my hon. friend, entertain suspicions, and perhaps even better founded than his. Apparently they entertained sorfie suspicions of Mr. Preston and put him in jail, and I understand he was in jail for five or six hours. Nothing very serious happened, except, I have been informed, that Mr. Preston was a little disturbed in his mind. I understand one of his fellow-prisoners was a jolly little Irishman, and, during the course of that brief incarceration, there were steps heard outside, and Mr. Preston asked in some apprehension what this thing was, and was told: " Don't worry yourself, it will soon be over; it is the firing squad."
My hon. friend next brought up a lot of charges which I must confess I had very great difficulty in following. His voice, while it rose at times to great passion and fervor, sometimes sank so low when he was reading that bewildering list of names, that I could scarcely hear him. As nearly as I could follow him, he was charging that there were a lot of votes transferred to different places such as Prince Edward county or elsewhere where they did not belong, and to Northumberland, and he read out, in fact, several pages of these things. He seemed to think that something terrible had been done; that this was further conclusive evidence of the deep-laid conspiracy which he was so fond of rolling under his tongue. But let me point out that in each case the vote was allocated to the place indicated on the ehvelope as the residence, not to the place where the man might want to vote or was trying to vote and should not. A widespread impression prevailed among the soldiers that they could elect what constituency they should vote in. Take the case of Prince Edward County, for instance. It is conceivable that a great .many men in the battalion of their

officer, Major Hepburn, who was a candidate for Prince Edward County, even if they did not belong to that county would have the impression that they could vote in the county of Prince Edward and would do all they could to persuade all the other fellows to vote there too if they could. But that does not imply that they did so.
Yes, they did.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Their votes were not
allocated there if they gave their residence as somewhere else.
They voted there.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Was the vote allocated to that constituency if the residence was given as somewhere else? Not at all, it was rejected.
Not all. Practically the whole battalion voted there.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
" historical notes." Well, to quote the . words used by the member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Butts) last night, " A rose by any other naim-e would smell as sweet." . I wish to touch upon another matter on which my hon. friend/ laid a good deal of stress and on which his friends and the chief scrutineer in- England, Mr. Preston, also laid stress-the alleged irregularities in connection with the ballot hags. He asserted that all kinds of ballots had been folded together and put in the ballot hags; that they had been put in one time, not in a proper way, and that they were of different dates. As this matter has been the subject of some discussion, I wish to deal with it somewhat fully. Charges also were made in respect of the envelopes from different camps. It was intimated that the officers at these camps, as well as the higher election officials, must have been cognizant of this. As evidence of the spirit in which Colonel Pnrney, Assistant Clerk of the Crown in Chancery overseas, conducted his operations, I wish to read a letter which he sent to the special officers Whom he was to assist by instruction and advice concerning the election laws, and so on, in the various polling places. It is as follows:
Dear Sir,-
If it were possible I would visit all points where voting at the ensuing Dominion election will be carried on. My chief objects in making such visits would be to satisfy myself without actually interfering with the work of the officials at the polls, that they have:
1. A thorough knowledge of the Military , Voters' Act and of the work they are carrying on.
,	2. That every effort is being made by them
to give every military elector in their district a chance to vote.
3. That" the instructions which have been sent out by me have been absolutely followed.
As it is physically impossible for me to make this visit personally I have asked for the services of officers to assist me in this work. You have been detailed to me as one of them and I would like you to understand that in carrying out your work you must be strictly non-partisan, not doing anything that could possibly be construed as being campaign work. The least departure from this necessary provision would mean your instant return to duty.
I would also like you to make it known throughout your district that you will be available to all officials, conducting the election within your area, for advice and instruction.
It is my desire that the full vote he polled and if there is any carelessness or a disposition on the -part of any official not to do this, you must report it immediately to this office.
I do not wish you to take from these 'blunt instructions, which I must necessarily give you, any inference that I have anything but the fullest confidence in your ability to do the work which I have appointed you to do. That is farthest from my mind. If I had not the
fMr. Burrell.]
utmost confidence in your willingness and ability to assist me in the heavy work which is imposed upon me, I would not have called upon you. It is, however, incumbent upon me, situated as I am, to lay down hard and fast instructions, such as I myself have to follow in the prosecution of my work, for those who are sharing my responsibilities.
I hope to make a hurried trip to the various districts where the votes are being polled.
That, I think, will commend, itself to the House as a proper spirit in which the chief and responsible officer should address all the men who are carrying on those elections.
Irregularities were charged in reference to the ballot -bags and envelopes, and the charges were especially directed/ to certain matters that went on at Witley Camp. The officer in charge at Witley Camp is Major-General Hughes, who is- known to many members in this House, and when the matter was called to his attention, he wrote this letter:
With reference to your letter of December 6th, 1917, enclosing a copy of a letter addressed to you from Mr. W. T. R. Preston.

That is a sample of many others, and I should like to say that, from my examination of the documents in question and from listening to my hon. friend's remarks, 1 have absolutely failed to see that there was any sufficient evidence in connection with this matter to impugn the honour and good faith of a large number of His Majesty's officers in the Canadian Expeditionary Forces who were trying to do their duty.
I shall, however, speak a little more about this matter of the bags because a good deal of stress has been laid upon it by my hon. friend. There were cases submitted. There was nothing to indicate in many cases that the bags had been, opened. It was urged that the best proof that they had been tampered with or opened was the fact that a number of those envelopes that were put in had become unrolled, flattened out and folded together, and looked, therefore, as though they had been put in at one time and subsequently to the proper day of voting. It is quite obvious that, as soon as envelopes containing ballots were dropped into a bag, _ they would become unrolled, and that many would gradually fit O'- fold together, as bags were hung up and, after the voting, put aside for weeks probably with other hags of considerable weight on the top of them. Naturally in such a case a number of the envelopes would become

pressed or folded together. In any case if a deputy presiding officer had allowed a few envelopes to collect, folded them together and inserted them in the bag at the same time, and even did so (not through the very small aperture provided for that purpose, but pushed them through the chained and locked mouth of the bag, which might not have been perfectly tight), there would have 'been nothing decidedly illegal ^bout that, as all such instructions in the Act as to how the envelope should be inserted, etc., were directory only. It would have been permissible to pqt the envelope in an open bag, or through the opening if a chained and locked bag. The instructions were not comprtlsory. But, however, there is no reason for believing that every envelope was not inserted through the aperture made for that purpose. - I want to put this on record. When a few bags had been laid aside on the grounds above stated, Colonel Purney caused the deputy presiding officers affected to be brought to London in order that the facts might be ascertained.	.
But this became a habit, and in England Mr. Preston, or other gentlemen .acting under him, began to urge that every bag looked as if it had been tampered with, and 'they not only objected to those bags being counted, but went the length of insisting that eVery bag should have the reason for its having been thrust aside marked on it; further that the. bag should be opened and that there should be marked on every envelope the reason for that bag having been set aside as being no good and even that the envelopes should be opened Aid the ballots so marked. If that practice had been pursued there would have been no such thing as an election and Parliament would not have sat here until the summer. The thing was so absurd and obviously for the purpose of delay that I do not wonder at the Overseas Clerk of the Crown in. Chancery in London becoming Impatient. He took advice on this matter, because he could see where it was leading to, and he sent this telegram dated January 22, to Mr. O'Connor, General Returning Officer, in this country:

That telegram sets forth the facts very well. I would point out to my hon. friend and the House that the policy which was adopted by the chief scrutineer and many of his subordinate officers was to insist on very slight evidence that bags had been tampered with and envelopes inserted in an improper manner, and yet precisely the same operation which took place in England took place here and took place also in France, and we never had a word of complaint, practically speaking, in France or Canada. The same objections, it is true, were raised in Canada, but after examination and after consultation bags were set aside, though not to anything like the same number, and afterwards a general agreement was come to and the votes were counted. _ It is perfectly plain that the wffiole object over 'there was to set aside an indefinite number of bags, and an effort was made to delay in a most extraordinary and unjustifiable way the progresg of the whole election. My hon. friend adduced as a reason that there was a conspiracy the fact that three or four envelopes of different dates were rolled together, and he argued that that was proof they had been put in improperly. I would say it proyed just the contrary, because it would have been stupid for a man who wanted to do such a thing as that to put together envelopes of different dates. Such a man would have been clever enough to make them all of the same date, so as to avoid being detected.
I do npt think I need delay the House any longer on that point.
My hon. friend has said that a great number of the soldiers voted twice. It is quite possible that some of the soldiers voted twice. - I think it has been quite possible in any election for a number of men to vote twice; you cannot always stop these things. But in regard to the military voters, if any of them did vote twice, wherever that was detected both votes were

rejected, and I think my hon. friend ought to know that. In regard to personating, I am not here to argue whether there was personating or not. I think it would he very difficult to trace out innumerable points of alleged irregularities ini an election of such extraordinary difficulties as the one held last December. I am hot saying whether personating was or was not done, but I am here to say that there was no double voting or personating to the extent that would justify my hon. friend in assuming that there was a dark and deep-laid conspiracy on the part of somebody unknown to do all these things.
I would point out, in closing, that the one obvious thing that sticks out in this whole matter is, that all these objections, all these charges and all these insinuations of deep and dark conspiracies, come from one place, from England. They do not come from France, and they have not been alleged in regard to Canada; and yet, I repeat, the administration by the election officials was carried on in precisely the same way, under precisely the same rulings and decisions In all three places, England, Canada and France. I would also like to emphasize again this fact in regard to the futility, to my mind, of wasting the time of the House on a subject of this kind in the manner my hon. friend has wasted it; the soldiers were so overwhelmingly in favour of conscription that the matters my hon. friend refers to are a mere bagatelle, an infinitesimal grain of sand, so far as they affect the general results of the mandate of the people as expressed in the last election.
'My hon. friend knows that from 90 to 85 per cent of the votes of soldiers that were counted, to say nothing of those that were rejected, were in favour of this Union Government and of conscription. As to what the feeling of the soldiers was, I particularly remember that during my election I went down to a certain station in British Columbia to meet 330 soldiers who had just come back from France. We were in the middle of the election and we were naturally anxious to know what the real feelings of the soldiers was in this grave national crisis. One man who got off the train was a stalwart Highlander of about 45 years of age, who had been at the front since 1914. I asked him if he knew what the general views were of the Union Government and of conscription. "Well," he said, " I do not know anything about Union Government, but as regard the other -matter, while I am not able to speak with regard to the feeling in England, I can say
that every man who has been in France is in favour of conscription and against prohibition." I have nothing to say about his views with respect to prohibition, but I got from him an impression of the strength of feeling that existed. What is it after all that has inspired the general attitude- what is it that has inspired my hon. friend in regard to England? It is impossible to avoid the conclusion that it is the personality of the chief election agent of my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, Mr. Preston. He raised, all through the conduct of affairs the most strenuous objection to the administration of the Act, to the officials and to everybody engaged in carrying out the Act, and he has hinted at and charged irregularities all along the line. He has made allegations of wholesale fraud which have not been substantiated, and he has made very strong charges about the unjustifiable partisanship that existed. I do not know that the gentleman in question is a very bad judge of partisanship. I do not think that anybody who knows the history of that gentleman will deny that he is a fairly strong partisan. It is no wonder that this type of man should be looking around all over England for some mysterious machine for running the election because he no doubt believes that is the way elections are run. He probably knows something about it, and he has a good deal of suspicion of other people with regard to election frauds.
I have alluded to one or two things that the hon. gentleman said in connection with that matter, but I would like to point out that Mr. Preston does show suspicion and my hon. friend does show suspicion of the work that was d-one in England by those who were responsible for the administration of this Act. My -hon- friend while reading innumerable affidavits read one of a gentleman named Mr. D'Arcy. It appears that Mr... D'Arcy was told that he would be sent right off to the front if he did not vote for Union Government, but he said he was going to vote for Laurier, that his father and his grandfather and his whole family had voted for my right hon. friend and that nothing could swerve him from his determination to vote for Laurier. He would' vote for Laurier and was against conscription. In the face of that statement and having in mind the source from which it emanated I desire to tell the House that I hold in my hand a newspaper bearing date December 11, 19K7. It is a newspaper called the Penrith Observer, a well known Welsh newspaper, and in a corner of that paper there appears, in large type, an ad-

vertisement addressed, " To the 'Canadian Overseas Forces ". This is signed by " W. T. R. Preston, on behalf of the Liberal candidates." How does the House think this advertisement is worded, and what is the heading? In big black letters, " Vote for Sir 'Wilfrid and Conscription and a Leader You can Trust."
See his statement at Ottawa, (London Press, Nov. 29th) in which he declares he will not ask Parliament to repeal the Compulsory Service Act. Training will therefore go on which will furnish a full quota of reinforcements.
Here is a man who is supplying my hon. friend with his ammunition, most of it based on the flimsiest evidence and talking about partisanship and everything of that kind, publishing over his own signature in a British paper an appeal to the soldiers to " vote for Lauriex and conscription " under the theory and belief that he will delude the soldiers into believing that if they supported my right hon. friend they would he voting in favour of conscription. This advertisement was published in face of the fact that my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition told the people of the West that he was not in favour of conscription. Lots of my right hon. friend's friends in the West had a very.loyal and affectionate regard for him and they gave him, as we Unionists gave him, a real welcome on account of his personality when he came to the West. There was no lack of courtesy there. There were a great many men who had suspended judgment upon my right hon. friend and who, although they approved of conscription, and rather approved of Unoin Government, hesitated to withhold their.votes from my right hon. friend because they - believed that he had been maligned in the party press', and that he had not said what he was reported to have said in regard to conscription. My right hon. friend came there and.told them where he stood. They went away with bowed heads and said.: " There is nothing for us to do but to leave him and to vote for Union-. Government, because he has put his position plainly before us." What was it that he put before us? He said' that he against conscription. It is true he said *{that he would not repeal the Act, but he *would suspend the operation of the Act, ireturn to the voluntary system, take a [DOT]referendum of the people and go out to the people himself and appeal against the whole theory of conscription. In the face of that here is this man putting an advertisement in a British paper and asking the soldiers fMr. Burrell.]
who are fighting our .battle in. Europe, who believe that conscription was the only way to get the necessary reinforcements to oppose the Hun, to " vote for Laurier and conscription." If that isi the authority to which my hon. friend appeals, I must say that he is discredited by that authority's own announcements.
I have to apologize to the House for speaking s.o long, but I want to close with this testimony. I think my hon. friend was rather unfortunate in his somewhat vague denunciation of everybody connected with the administration of the Act, and in suggesting that the officials were more or less cognizant of those things which he charged, that they tolerated and connived at them. It may be .a surprise to the House to know that the gentleman who advertised this appeal in that way is the person who supplied my hon. friend with his ammunition and supplied him, I presume, with those lengthy lists of names, which really need not have been put on Hansard, because they did not substantiate anything in connection with this matter. This same gentleman wrote a letter and I am going to read it. This is a letter to Colonel Purney in reply to the suggestion, and it is dated November 23, 1917:

November 23rd, 1917. My dear Colonel Purney,-
In reply to the suggestion that the advertisement in to-day's issue of Canada might possibly be interpreted .or taken as a reflection upon your position as assistant cleric of the Crown in Chancery, and your staff, permit me to say that the reference to officers is entirely in regard to those who had received instructions from the Government at Ottawa to canvass and organize the overseas forces on -behalf of the Government, and to do their utmost to secure the election of the Government candidates in certain constituencies, a, list of which instructions had been given should be placed in their hands.
Speaking on behalf of the Liberal candidates I desire to say that instead of there being a suspicion that you would not act impartially, there is, without exception, a unanimous opinion that your integrity is unimpeachable, and that you will discharge your duties with the most strict impartiality, and that no partiality on the part of any of your appointees will be tolerated by you.

I have only to say in closing, that to those who are chiefly concerned in this matter, any difficulties, any irregularities, or any breach of the technicalities of the law, which have occurred,-and which must necessarily occur to some extent in any election, and which it would be impossible to avoid in an election so extraordinary as that which has just taken place,-have not been sufficient to justify the general and broad charge of conspiracy that my hon. friend has made, and on the whole I think this House will agree with me, that as far as the administration of 'the Act goes, and as far as regards the fulfilment of the purpose which the Government and this House had in mind,-namely, to give the military electors of Canada, and all those who are fighting our battles, a fair right to express their opinion in regard to the destinies of this country,-I think that purpose was fulfilled with few blemishes and with an honest and sincere desire on "the part of the officials to carry out their duties, and I think with a reasonable and fair measure of success.

Mr. Speaker, I was not at all surprised to-night when I saw the Secretary of State (Mr. Burrell) rise, to answer in the name of the Government the charges made by my hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. Copp) on the military vote. No one else in the Cabinet could have replied, as the hon. minister is probably the only Simon-pure on this 'subject, and probably the only member of the Government who did not commit himself last year when the Military Voters Bill was discussed in the House. Looking through Hansard,
I find that the Secretary of State did not speak on this question on that occasion. The other members of the Government, if I am right, did commit themselves, but, Sir, how differently. Some of those hon. gentlemen, like the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers) indignantly repudiated' the idea that frauds could be committed in relation to the Act, or that it could be used in the interest of the Union Government. But others, like the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell) and the present Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Maclean) _ denounced the Act in question most vigor ously. I have not time to read the whole of their utterances, but it may be of some interest to the House to quote just one extract from the speech of the Acting Minister of Finance, which I find at page 4716 of the Revised Hansard of last year:
Subsection 2 of section 3 requires that a voter, on presenting himself, must state the electoral district wherein he last resided, during a restricted period at least. Then there is another provision to the effect that if he cannot state or specify a residence he shall be deemed an elector from such electoral district as he may indicate. Supposing he had never been in Canada prior to his enlistment. Imagine the case of his proceeding overseas the day after he enlisted. Theoretically at least he would not know the name of a single electoral district in 'Canada. Take a case put to me after six o'clock this evening by a member of this House whose next opponent is an officer commanding a Canadian regiment in France. Say that, of 1 000 men, 999 oame from the colony of Newfoundland and the 'British West Indies, and that they did not know any of the electoral districts of Canada; it would be quite evident that they could not state the electoral district in which they resided continuously for a certain period in Canada, because they had never resided here. They could not indicate any electoral district to which they desired their vote allocated. What would be the consequence? They would be entirely under the domination of their commanding officer. I do not say that would happen, I have no fear whatever of any improper influence being exerted in the taking of these votes overseas. But I submit that, when you point out the possibilities for the exercise of improper in-

fluences, you thereby point out fundamental weaknesses in the Bill, and we, as representatives of the people, seriously considering-an important piece of legislation, are bound to take that into consideration.
I do not believe, Mr. Speaker, it is necessary to reply to the speech of my hon. friend the Secretary of State, because at the beginning of his remarks he stated that even if all the charges- made by the hon. member- for Westmorland were true, it did not matter, because the Union Government was elected without the military vote. To such a conception of political morality, Mr. Speaker, it is useless to answer. I 'may say, though, that my hon. friend was right when he stated candidly that in his opinion there was a universal impression that the military voter could apply his vote in any constituency he desired. It is an admission, indeed, that when the Government secured the passage of this Act last year, and when the present Minister of Public Works and the Acting Minister of Finance denounced it, expressing their fear that the Government could use that vote for improper purposes, my hon. friends who are now on the treasury benches, but who were then on this side of the House, were right iu the fear to which they gave expression.
The Secretary of State has seen fit to make a charge against a son-in-law of Mr. Preston. I am not aware of the facts which he has related, but it seems to me that, the making of such an accusation is a pretty good reason why we should have an inquiry. The Secretary of State will then have ample opportunity to .air his charges properly and legally, and we, on this side, will not prevent him from punishing the guilty whether the man is a Liberal or a Unionist. My hon. friend also said that there were no accusations from Canada or France, but only from England. Let me tell him that it is not my intention-
The Secretary of State has left the chamber.

His. friends will tell him what I s-ay. Let me state that it is not my intention to review the votes cast generally by the soldiers overseas or in North America, because I have not made a study of that vote. But the present discus-s-ion gives me the opportunity of bringing before the House a special case of conspiracy carried out, not overseas, not in France, or in England, but in the military barracks at St. Johns, Quebec) during the last general election, which only emphasizes the necessity of having an [Mr. Arcbambaultl
inquiry in relation to the whole military vote. I have tried, Mr. Speaker, unsuccessfully since the beginning o-f the session, to bring this matter up, and in this connection let me assure the Secretary of State that my ammunition does not come from the source which he dislikes so much. On the 16th of last month I placed on the Order Paper a motion calling for:
A copy of envelopes Nos. 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, 15, 17, 19, 20, 21, 2.2, 3'9, 53, 56, 59 and 99, polling booth No. 9, Barracks of St. Johns, Quebec, used in the Federal Election of 17th December last and placed in Military bag No. 446 of the North American Continent Military Votes. Also, a copy of the envelopes Numbers 05 and 70, polling booth No. 4, Barracks of St. Johns, Quebec, used in the Federal Election of 17th December last, and placed in Military bag Number 451 of the North American Continent Military Votes.
To this, motion, when I proposed to move it, the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) said, " Stand." On the 22nd- of April my motion was still on the Order Paper, and when I -was about to proceed with it the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) expressed some doubt as to the possibility of producing the documents asked for, and begged to be allowed to examine more closely into the effect of the motion before it was passed-. On 1st May the motion was called again and the Minister of Justice stated that the reasons he had given on April 22nd appeared sufficient to refuse the production o:f such papers. However, the motion was again allowed to stand. My next move was to drop the motion, believing that, perhaps, the phraseology was not regular. I had asked for the production of documents-, which had been placed in ballot bags. I was informed- later on that the documents had been taken from those ballot bags and placed in ballo-t boxes. Therefore, I put in another motion asking for the same envelopes, papers and documents that had been originally put into ballot bags, but later on had been transferred to ballo-t boxes. To the latter motion the Prime Minister again said " Stand." Finding that the Government was unwilling to grant my request, I said: Since the Government does not seem disposed to grant this motion, as I believe they should, I shall withdraw' it, hut I give notice that I will bring the matter before the House at the first opportunity. This is the subject which I wish to bring up to-night. It is with a great deal of reluctance, Mr. Speaker, that I br-ng it forward, and I must say that before taking this step I gave the question very careful consideration. My election not having been

I repeat that this paper was published and distributed throughout the barracks against the King's regulations and orders, which provide that no political meeting shall be held or political publication distributed in barracks where soldiers are quartered. This issue of December 15th, page 12, has also the following:
One vital issue; For the first time in the history of Canada public opinion is sharply divided on a single, vital issue. Shall we or shall we not send reinforcements to those heroic Canadians, who, during the past three long years, have played such a gallant part in making it possible for you and for me to live in safety and in comfort?
On the one hand are those indomitable Canadian battalions which, at Ypres and St. Julian, at Messines, Vimy and on numberless bloody fields have brought immortal fame to the name of Canada.
On The Left Hand-
And on the other side what do we find? Cowardly mobs who, at Sherbrooke, at Montreal, at Quebec and at a score of other places, have attempted and still attempt to impose German brutality and mob violence on the people of Canada; Germans and avowedly pro-Germans who at Kitchener and elsewhere, have attempted to disgrace the name of Canada in the eyes of the world; slackers who would stand idly by and see their women folk suffer the unspeakable fate of the women of France and Belgium rather than play a man's part beside the heroes who are to-day fighting their battles.
_ In the past, in civil life, you have been accustomed to choose your friends and associates; your selection has reflected your true character. Now you are confronted by a choice of supremest importance.
And what will be your choice?

Section 170 says:
Perjury is an assertion as to a matter of fact, opinion, belief or knowledge, made by a witness in a judicial proceeding as part of his evidence, upon oath or affirmation, whether such evidence is given in open court, or by affidavit or otherwise, and whether such evidence is material or not, such assertion being known to such witness to be false, and being intended by him to mislead the court, jury or person holding the proceeding.
Subornation of perjury is counselling or procuring a person to commit any perjury which is actually committed.
'Section 172 says:
Every one is guilty of perjury who,____
(a) having taken or made any oath, affirmation, solemn declaration or affidavit whereby any Act, or law in force in Canada, or in any province of Canada, it is required or permitted that facts, matters or things be verified, or otherwise assured or ascertained by or upon the oath, affirmation, declaration or affidavit of any person, wilfully and corruptly, upon such oath, affirmation, declaration or affidavit, deposes, swears to or makes any false statement as to any such fact, matter or thing.
Section 175 says:
Every one is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to seven years' imprisonment who, being required or authorized by law to make 
any statement on oath, .affirmation or solemn declaration, thereupon makes ' a statement which would amount to perjury if made in a judicial proceeding.

My first intention when I had in my hands the evidence of what took place at St. Johns was to institute criminal proceedings against Col. W. W. Melville and his assistants.
Do it yet.

I am not making a threat, but I must say it will be my only alternative; that I will lay a complaint if nothing is done by the Government in that regard.
But I wish to point out that I believe it is the duty of the Government to have a thorough inquiry into this matter, not only into what happened in my constitusncy, but into the whole military vote, and I gladly second the motion made by my hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. Copp). The Government should be just as anxious
More so.

-as I am, for the honour and good name of our army, to make a full search into all these facts and to get rid of officers who, instead of giving to their subordinates an example of righteousness, honour and God's fear, fell so low as to perjure * themselves1, and what is worse, used their influence to induce their men to do so. Sir, officers with that standard of morality are liable to betray their country before the enemy if they ever go to the front, and they should be cashiered at once. Crime is the antithesi? of patriotism.
Mr. Speaker, at this late hour I do not wish to take up much of the time of the House-
The answer of the Government.

Ten ,minutes, I think, will do me to answer all that has been said here to-night. I started in to do a little figuring while the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. iOopp) was speaking, and I think I have now got my figures right. I figured that the speech of the hon. member for Westmorland had cost the country, as closely as I could get to the correct amount, valuing the time of hon. members at one dollar an hour and the time of the spectators in the gallery at fifty cents an hour, somewhere in the neighbourhood of $2,350.35. I do not think I would be striking my hon. friend too hard if I said that this House could go up to Sparks street and go tnto the Woolworth building and get for fifteen cents more knowledge than it has received from my hon. friend from Westmorland. The hon. member for Chamibly and Verchere-s (Mr. .Archambault) gave us quite a little entertainment. He exhibited considerable eloquence, but I think at the same time I would be very slow to tell such a tale about my constituency as he has told' about his. He says that in one day there were 700 perjurers in his constituency.
Not in my constituency.
The hon. member said St. Johns, Quebec; Chambly and Vercheres is what he told us about.

My constituency is Chambly and Vercheres, but St. Johns is outside of that constituency. The barracks are situated at St. Johns, Quebec, in the county of St. Johns and Iberville, and not one of the soldiers came from Quebec.

None of them
-were from my province.
'Mr. BUTTS:	If he did- not bring his
criminals to justice, why did he not appeal to his Attorney General to see that the fair name of his province was not blackened in such a manner, instead of coming here and telling as to-night about the perjuries and the crimes that seem rampant in his constituency?
In that four - hours - and-five-minutes s-peec'h that cost this country, apart from the expenses of Hansard and printing, something over $2,300, the hon. m-ember for Westmorland sipoke of votes from Sydney Alines and Glace Bay being counted in constituencies in Quebec, and perhaps in Ontario. I d-o not think that any of my hon. friends have very much right or reason in their cause when they began to co-mplain about the election. They got 62 out of 65 seats -in Quebec. How much more do they want? Do they want the world with a fen-ce around it? My h-on. friend spoke of Sydney Mines and Glace Bay, and those are two towns above all in Canada that I can speak of with some knowledge.
A short time ago I resigned my position of town solicitor and stipendary magistrate of the town of Sydney Mines, a position I

had held for nineteen years. In that town ' of nearly ten thousand people I have three brothers who have been elected as town councillors, -and whenever they have run they have never been beaten. There is hardly a man in the whole town that I cannot shake hands with and call by name. My hon. friend has spoken of men from Sydney Mines polling their votes in counties in the province of Quebec. Now, I do not wish to violate the Criminal Code, I do not want to get into trouble for gambling, but if my hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. Copp) will hand me a list of these men from Sydney Mines I will put a -five dollar bill over every name, if he will put another one, and every time ;I win I take the ten dollars and he can have the ten dollars every other time. I do not think my hon. friend is game enough to take that up. He has either to put up or shut up.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am afraid the language of the hon. member is hardly in conformity with the custom of Parliament.

I bow to your ruling, Mr. Speaker, hut it did work me up a little bit when my hon. friend spoke of these voters from two towns in my own county. I know there cannot possibly be any justification for it, because I know that eveTy one of those men in Sydney Mines whom he alleges to have voted in the province of Quebec would have been only too glad to use their votes against my hon. friend from North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) and every man in -Glace Bay would have been only too glad to vote for myself or my colleague, Mr. John Douglas.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) :
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The motion which the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. iCopp) has made, he puts before this House under the guise simply of a motion- asking for -an inquiry into certain, matters which he laid before this House at very considerable length this afternoon. He does that, however, by means of a motion in amendment to the motion to go' into Supply, which in practical effect means that upon charges, none of them directed against this Government and by none of which he makes any imputation upon any member of this Government or upon any action of this Government, he asks this House to vote want, of confidence in this Government. There was open to the hon. gentleman, and it has been open to him throughout this entire session, a perfectly direct method of bringing the charges he has seen proper to bring and asking for the investigation that he desires. He did not choose
to avail himself of that method, but at this last moment of the session he makes this motion in the form of a motion of want of confidence, and asks this House in effect to vote want of confidence in the present Government. He interposes 'between the making and the granting of his request for an investigation the necessity of adopting that vote of want of confidence in the Government. It is needless to say that in adoptihg that course the conclusion is inevitable that the hon. gentleman could not have expected the acceptance of this motion on the part of this Government, and therefore he could not have hoped by means of this particular motion to arrive at the investigation for which he has asked.
The subject matter in itself is undoubtedly one of great gravity. It is a subject of all subjects, I think, that must be approached, eliminating from its consideration party interest or party advantage, and above all not involving in its decision the fate of a Government which I have no hesitation in saying enjoys^ the confidence, it is perfectly manifest, of a great majority of the members of this House, and certainly anything that was said this afternoon, whatever may be the truth or the falsehood of the accusations brought against any particular individuals, was not of a nature to shake that confidence. I know of no motion that could be more aptly described as a non sequitur than this particular motion, but, as I have said, the subject matter of this motion is certainly of great gravity. The hon. member who made this motion took up a long period of the time of this House-in what? In bringing most grave and serious charges against men who are our fellow-citizens, men who to-day are not here in this country to make any answer on their behalf to his charges because they are engaged in the great and paramount, work of the defence of this country. Now I think that when, as he said-and I assume he was speaking sincerely when he said it-in the performance of what he conceived to be his duty he thought it proper to lay these charges, it was at least incumbent upon him to do it in such a manner as would assure the attainment of the purpose which he states he has in view, and without involving the result which this motion must first attain in order to arrive at the object of an inquiry where these men would be afforded opportunity of reply. The hon. gentleman has made use of an ex parte' statement. He tells this House that it rests upon evidence that satisfies him. He does not tell us how long he ha*

been in jjos'session of that evidence. Presumably, it is not yesterday, and he has allowed this session to run through and has not taken the steps that might have been open to him at an earlier period to bring about, perhaps, an immediate investigation.
I do not intend to go into the discussion of the well or ill-foundedness of the charges and accusation made by the hon. member for Westmorland. It would be impossible for any man immediately upon hearing these charges, coming as they came to us this afternoon, to arrive at any satisfactory conclusion not only as to their truth or falseness, but even upon the question as to whether or not there was -a prima facie case made out against any of the individuals whom he so seriously impeached. The hon. gentleman asks us to order a judicial investigation not merely of the particular charges that he madte, but of the entire taking of the soldiers' votes. The charges he made, as has been pointed out, are entirely charges of misconduct on the part of officers and men, who, at the time they are alleged to have committed these offences, were stationed in England. Many of these men, if not all of them, to- . day, have gone forward. He recognized that himself in his motion because he feels the necessity of withdrawing from the judge whom he asks to have appointed to investigate the power of summoning witnesses whose presence would interfere with the performance of their duties as soldiers.
What is this so-called remedy that he aske for the condition of affairs that he has described? Let me deal with it as he dealt with it, in so far as it would be applicable, in so far as it calls for judicial investigation at the present moment and held in England, into the conduct of the election so far as military voters were concerned, and so far as that election was Held in England. I think the House is satisfied, after the exposition of my hon. friend and colleague, the Secretary of State (Mr. Burrell) that in the taking of that election, on the whole, and by and large, it was fairly and honourably conducted. If the particular charges that are made here to-night were true it would not alter the fact that upon the whole, on the evidence we have before us, we are in no position to say that there is ground to suspect that there were any general irregularities throughout that election. Such an investigation in England, at the present time, for the purpose of clearing up these charges which the hon. member for Westmorland would make, must, in the first place, involve the most serious possible ineonven-

ience and interference with the military operations on the other side, an interference and obstruction that could only he justified by its being established that some adequate, effective result would be obtained by that investigation. I did not understand that, by either of the hon. gentlemen who spoke, it was contended that any of the irregularities that they alleged affected in any way either the general result of the election, or even the result of the election in any particular constituency. Had it been so contended, one would naturally have expected that a remedy other than that which is sought by the present motion would have been asked or. I think the form of the present motion goes to confirm the impression gathered from what was said in support of it that there is no contention that either the election as a whole or the election in any particular constituency was affected by the irregularities charged, either upon the other side of _ the Atlantic or upon this side. Were there any such contention it is obvious that the proposed remedy would afford no correction of any unjustified result in any particular election. What, then, is the purpose that could be obtained? It would be the maintenance of these charges if the ihon. gentleman is right in his contention. Is it of sufficient importance that at the present time, with all the difficulties that would be in the way of a satisfactory investigation, with the necessary interference that such an investigation must bring about in the military operations on the other side, we should ascertain whether these charges without affecting in any way the result of any election, are, or are not ill founded?
When the suggestion was made from this side that these alleged offences did not affect the result of the election, we were treated with some expressions as to our standard of morality on this side of the House. I do not think there is implied any suggestion-and certainly on my part there is intended no-such suggestion-that because these alleged irregularities and this misconduct, if they took place, did not affect the result of the election, they are not to be seriously condemned.
