But is it of sufficient importance at the present moment, if this motion he carried, to justify our setting on foot an investigation, which, as I have said, must necessarily be carried on in the face of insuperable difficulties and obstacles which most assuredly must constitute a serious interference with the regular carrying on of military operations? For the reason, therefore, that I have

pointed out, I think it is impossible for any one not ready to declare his lack of confidence in this Government, because certain military officers acting as election officers may have misbehaved themselves, to vote for this motion requiring us to crder an investigation because the investigation, if it were ordered and held at the present moment, would afford no effective remedy in any way for any wrong or any evil committed by any person in this- country or in any constituency of this country by reason of its being represented by one who was not lawfully elected. The only purpose that might be obtained immediately and now, whether certain officers are or are not deserving of condemnation is not a purpose which would justify our resorting to the method which has been suggested, and therefore it seems to me we would clearly not be justified in adopting the present motion, even if it stood as a substantive motion, and in asking for an investigation of the kind, that is sought into the operations in connection with the election as held in England and in France.
Now the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault) has laid before us to-night what he claims to know to be facts with regard to the election as it was carried on among the soldiers in the constituency which he represents. It may be -I think it is-perfectly fair to point out when he expresses such grave indignation concerning what he alleges to he the conduct of certain officers in the barracks at St. Johns, and such severe condemnation of those officers in themselves, that he, in possession of all this information-and let me say in that regard that I agree with him, if his statement be true, if his statement be well founded, and I do not mean to suggest that he himself does not believe in their truth-and notwithstanding his indignation against those who, in his belief, are guilty of this very grave misconduct, has retained that information through all these months, and notwithstanding the knowledge that he has had up to this time hut has only imparted to us to-night, has never felt that there was any duty upon him to take the proceedings that it was oipen to him to take to vindicate the law and to impose upon those gentlemen to whom' he imputes such-very grave misconduct, the condign punishment that their conduct, if they are guilty, would deserre. He referred to the fact that he had. moved for the production of certain envelopes used in the election in the county of Chambly-Vercheres, and he was scandalized because it was pointed out
to him that under the provisions of the Dominion Elections Act those documents, whether in the original hags or in the final ballot box in which they were deposited, were contained in a sealed receptacle, in regard to. which the law enjoined that the seals should be broken only in the presence of the tribunals mentioned in the Act and produced before those tribunals only upon the order of the judge presiding over them, and that only when there was either an election contestation or a charge of some kind in which the documents were necessary as evidence, could such order be given -(because this was pointed out to him, and because, furthermore, his attention was specially called to the fact that it was necessary to go into the question of the right or power of this House to- order the breaking of those seals and the production of those documents, because he had laid no charge before this House; no charge was made before the House into the investigation whereof those documents would be necessary)-because those things were pointed out to him, representations in which he acquiesces by dropping his motion, he seems to think that those incidents and the action of the Government in regard to them are in some way connected with these charges he has brought for the first time to-night, although he might have had them before the House at an earlier date, when a satisfactory method of dealing with them might have been proposed. I am not going into this question now: it is certainly not possible we should deal with them in that way now, and this motion does not ask that we should do so. Eliminating for a moment the form of the motion-which makes it, as I have pointed out, absolutely unacceptable, and necessarily so-that motion asks for a general investigation into the entire elections so far as regards the extent to which the military vote was poMed. The hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres, as' ground for his support of that motion, limits himself to making these very grave charges against the officers in command, I think, of a regiment of engineers, who were at the St.. Johns barracks during the election. 1 am not here to plead any extenuation of the offences which he has alleged those gentlemen were guilty of. Neither am I here to say, on the ex parte statement that we have heard this evening, that these men were guilty of those offences; but in so far as that particular charge is concerned, or series of charges, against that particular
24G2

group of men-which charges are brought to our knowledge to-night for the first time -I am quite prepared to say that if the evidence of which the hon. gentleman is in possession -and of which we are not in possession, makes a prima facie case in support of those charges, they should form the subject of a most thorough investigation. In. fact, if the evidence which the hon. gentleman has and which we have not, makes a prima facie case against the men whose names he"has mentioned, it would seem to. me that that evidence constitutes a better foundation for a prosecution for those grave offences than for a judicial investigation, which can, after all, be nothing else but a preliminary inquiry. But I am quite prepared to say-I do not want to make any distinctions-that at the least they are a proper subject matter for judicial inquiry.
And as regards this case which has been brought to our attention, when this House has disposed of this motion in the only way which is open to this House, which by its large majority has confidence in this Government, and which has heard this *evening nothing impugning or attacking this Government or affording ground for any lack of confidence in this Government -when I say, this House shall have disposed of the motion which is now before us in the only way which it is open to a House composed as is this House to dispose of it, that is by rejecting it,-the Government will, nevertheless, realize, as we all realize now, the propriety of there being investigation into the case that had been laid before us-judicial investigation.
When?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As promptly as that can be done.. Let me say this: I do not want to introduce into this discussion anything that might give it any tinge of bitterness. But I am glad to believe that it was thoughtlessness, but it was most painful, I am sure -it certainly was most painful to me, and I am sure, when my hon.. friends on the other side come to think it over, it will be painful for them,-to remember that they sat here this evening and cheered to the echo the evidence which, if it was true, would show that certain of our soldiers have shown themselves unworthy of the confidence that this Parliament reposed in them. When the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault) brought out what he considered this conclusive evidence, it was met by the resounding cheers of gentlemen upon the other side.
IMr. Doherty]
Surely, when they come to think it over, they with us all, if these men are guilty, will be sorry that these men should have been guilty. I am sure, after all, they, with all of us, would be glad if, notwithstanding the evidence which the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres informed us he Had in his possession, it should be found that there was some explanation of this conduct that would make it consistent with innocence on the part of these men.
And let me say this: I do not want to prejudge the case-it is easy to run away with the most condemnatory conclusions. Sometimes you find that, even in what appear to be strong prima facie cases, your first impression was very much mistaken.
I am not going to discuss the propriety of the publication of this newspaper which we had to read here, nor am I going to go into the question whether the opinions expressed in it were well or ill founded; nor whether they were expressed in just the language that would be considered most desirable. I do not want to prejudge now a case that is to be the subject matter of investigation by others. But, after all, if we all of us look back to the past election, and to elections which preceded it, shall we not perhaps- realize that under t'he influence of strong conviction the language of some of us has perhaps been as strong as the language that was read from that newspaper? There was the difference in the last election that exists between men of strong convictions when they differ on .a question of first importance. And I think we should all of us be willing to forgive, even to the soldier, wihat may appear to us sitting here this evening to be perhaps the exaggerated expression of a strongly-entertained conviction, that appealed after all, whether he was right or wrong, to his profound sense of devotion to our common country.
As to the charges that are made as to the conduct of the election itself, we heard very positive affirmations of perjury and subornation of perjury. These are grave charges. The hon. gentleman, no doubt, believes that he is in possession of the evidence to substantiate them, which moved him to throw all this matter before this House to-night, I do not say with the purpose but with the necessary result, that the men that he has accused here to-night must remain under suspicion until someone initiates proper proceedings that will lead to their condemnation or to their exoneration; and, -as I have pointed out already, he might have, carried these serious *'.harges

to a tribunal -where both sides could be heard and where the public would have had an opportunity of knowing in a reasonable way whether those charges were well or ill founded. Now we have heard this absolute assertion of . perjury and subornation of perjury. I am not here pleading for these men; I do not know what the circumstances were; I know nothing of them1 beyond what the hon. gentleman has told' us. But I do know this of my own personal knowledge, that many and many an honest man, absolutely an honest man in the province of Quebec, believed that under the Military Voters Act it was the privilege of the soldier to choose his constituency. And how w.as that belief brought about? By the persistent assertion, by the persistent mis-statement, coming from almost every platform of the party in opposition to this Government, that that was the state of the law. I spent much of my time in the course of that election making it clear to people that that was not the state of the law-perfectly honest people who had been misled into that belief by those who, being interested as they all were to bring about my defeat in particular, and the defeat of this Government as a whole, were industriously engaged in charging me with being the author of a law that told the soldier; "You can vote anywhere you please." And gentlemen who sowed that seed are astounded and indignant when there comes back to them what I do hot say in this particular case was, but what-very well in this case may have been, the result of the doctrine that they themselves had been preaching. It may be that all of these men committed perjury. It may be that many *of them acted in the honest belief that they were entitled to vote at the place that they selected.
Before we come to absolute condemnations, it would be well for us to know that these men were sworn at all. If things were as irregular as they are said to have been, it is not impossible that these soldiers were not sworn. If so, these wholesale charges, of perjury are certainly unfounded. I have not said these things because I want to defend these men if they be guilty, or because I want to prejudge the question whether they be innocent or guilty. When hon. gentlemen adopt a method of bringing these charges to the public which gives no opportunity of reply to the men accused, .some one should joint out in the meantime that it would, be well for the public to withhold their judgment. To-night we Are asked for an investigation; but the
whole tone of the ground upon which the investigation is asked for is the condemnation as guilty without further proceeding of the men against whom the charges are brought. I have no desire to introduce any feeling into this discussion; matters of this, kind are bigger than parties and bigger than governments and ought to be regarded from both sides and in as judicial a frame of mind as we are capable of bringing ourselves into. But in view of the fact that so many methods were open of bringing about a clear and satisfactory investigation followed by proper punishment or deserved exoneration, all fair-minded men will regret, with me, that the method adopted, which must be unfair to the accused, should have been considered the proper one. I think it is generally conceded that it is the duty of a good citizen, when he has information justifying the belief that crime has been committed, to lay that information before those who are charged with the enforcement of criminal law, and thus set the law in motion. But as the hon. member for Chambly and Ver- . cheres has not seen fit to adopt that course, and has-for what reason I am at a loss to imagine, because I should not like to impute to him any motive that I should not wish to have imputed to myself in like circumstances - adopted this particular method, the Government will take the steps that may be necessary to bring about judicial investigation of the case that has been put before us in this way to-night.
In what way?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That has been put before us by the member for Chambly and Vercheres; this case that is alleged to have happened in Canada and that it is. therefore, possible for us to deal with directly.
Will the inquiry toe limited to that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As far as I can say,
the inquiry will be limited to. the case that is 'brought before us. If other hon. gentlemen have other oases in which they can show us that there is cause for inquiry, we shall be glad to inquire.
Then you will grant an investigation, right away?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As regards the case that has been put before us.
With regard to the motion now before the House?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
With regard to this case of Chambly and Vercheres which has been

put before the House this evening. Let us have no misunderstanding; we will see that it is properly and judiciously investigated. As to the incidents referred to as having happened in, England, I have given sufficient reasons why it would be highly improper, even if we could hope to arrive at any practical result, to embark upon an investigation in England and France, the bulk of the necesary witnesses in which would be men who have other work to- do than that of giving testimony (before the courts, whether to inculpate their comrades or to exonerate themselves. In respect of the matter put before us by the member for Westmorland this ^evening, individual cases may justify some action in the way of further inquiry, and, perhaps, the taking of some measure looking to the disciplining of officers who may have been guilty of some offences. Should that he so, some action from this Government may toe called for, even in England. But of one thing the House can rest assured-: that the Government has no desire to cloak any guilty man or to encourage any of its officers in violation of the law. In saying that, I do not say that there was made to us this- afternoon a ease that would justify our ordering an inquiry in such a large and general way as has been suggested.
The Government feels that this is a motion with regard to which only one course is open to it and to those who have confidence in it. The Government realizes also the duty that has come to it with regard to this matter of Ohambly and Vercheres and is alive to such duty as may come to it, in proper cases and under proper circumstances', to look into charges involving the due performance of duty on the part of its officers, with an eye to such disciplining as circumstances may call for. But we should be doing anything but the work we are here to do if we cast over our forces overseas at this moment a general dragnet to see whether or not we might gather into it some soldier who had been guilty of some misdemeanour, some irregularity, or even some serious offence. If there be soldiers of that kind there will be time and place for dealing with them.

Mr. Speaker, when a man walking along the street finds that some one has unsuccessfully attempted to purloin his pocket-book, he is apt to be almost as angry with the intended thief as he would have been had the attempt been successful. I am one of the candidates who was marked out by the

Union Government to be defeated. I dv not know how many ministers in the present Government formed part of the Unionist organization. '
Two.

Had the plans laid
by the Unionist organization been successful, I would not have had the pleasure of [DOT]meeting hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House in friendly converse in the *corridor or have had the honour of representing the constituency I represent in this *House. I shall endeavour, as I trust there is no bitterness in my make-up, to follow the suggestion of the Minister Of Justice (iMr. Doherty) to discuss this case in the calmest and most judicial manner possible.
The Secretary of State (Mr. Burrell) addressed the House at some length. His main objection to the 'speech made by the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Copp) was that it was too long. His second objection was that those irregularities which had happened across the seas were irregularities which must have happened by inadvertence or carelessness, and the fact that many military voters had forgotten to answer questions Nos. 6, 7 and 8, was to be put down only to the feebleness of human memory and not to any ulterior or improper motive. The Secretary of State, after attacking the plantiff's attorney, also attacked one Of the plaintiff's witnesses.
I do not think the character of that witness is in issue here to-night. What is before the House is- a statement made toy an hon. member of this House, seconded toy another hon. member, that they believe that oertain irregularities and frauds were committed in connection with the taking of the soldiers' vote, and they ask for an investigation. They have brought before the House certain facts which, in my opinion, make out in many respects a prima facie case for an investigation. Apart from that, we have had a very able exposition of the electoral crimes- committed in the barracks at St. Johns, Quebec. Those have so impressed the Government that the Government has promised an investigation into them!. Would I be unfair in laying down this principle?-that, if I show that similar actions are likely to have occurred elsewhere, in connection, for instance, with my own election, that a similar investigation should toe granted into that, and if I showed that the facts make out a prima facie case that those irregularities and frauds were general, I make out [DOT] a case that the investigation should be

general and not confined to one particular case? I think I do.
The Minister of Justice says that the hon. member for Westmorland could not have expected his motion to carry. Why not? If there are serious grounds for believing that irregularities and electoral crimes v. ere committed in connection with the taking of the soldiers' vote, either across the seas or in Canada, why should not this Government grant an investigation? We have been told, with a modesty so peculiar to this present Government, that it represents, as the President of the Council has told us, the best elements in both parties. Surely the best elements in both parties will not allow any doubt to be cast upon the purity of their escutcheon. Surely, if any reasonable grounds for granting an investigation are brought before the House, they will hasten to show that they are true and honest men, above reproach. Why should we, on this side of the House, expect that the motion made by the hon. member for Westmorland should be defeated? The Minister of Justice referred to the fact that those men who are charged with having committed those irregularities-to follow the example of the Minister of Justice, we shall call things by their pleasantest names -are soldiers. We know that. We are not suggesting to the Government what punishment they should mete out to those men if they are found guilty. It may be and it certainly is true that, as far as the private soldiers were concerned, they were not free agents to begin with, and many of them will now, by their efforts, by their spilt blood upon the field, have expiated any commission of an offence. But I shall ask the Minister of Justice-does he lay down the principle that because a man is a soldier he is relieved of his moral responsibility towards his fellow Canadian citizens? I do not accept that. That has never been the manner in which the British people have looked upon the responsibility of their soldiers. I would go back to history and say that one of the greatest soldiers that ever commanded a British Army in the field, John Churchill, was once accused of serious crimes, and was very heavily punished. But now a more serious argument is brought forward by the Minister of Justice. He says: You cannot have such an investigation as you propose, without seriously interfering with military operations in the field. On the face of it, that is a serious objection if it is well founded in fact. But is that the case? The soldiers, when they voted; all placed on their envelopes, if their ballots were counted, the place where they lived in Canada, or they stated that they did not live in Canada at all. Those envelopes are in the possession of the Government. The ballots are in the possession of the Government. The names and addresses of the soldiers are in the possession of the Government. The whole investigation may, in very large measure, be made by an examination of the envelopes and the ballot papers which are in the possession of the Government. That course was followed in connection with the British Columbia soldiers' vote, and it is a matter of interest to this House to recollect that a precisely similar investigation was held under a commission appointed by the British Columbia Government, and .that by examination of the voting papers and the envelopes, they were able to determine that out of a total of 8,488 military votes, 3,796 were legitimate. What the British Columbia Government did was to cast aside the soldiers votes and refuse to accept them, because there had been such wholesale misconduct in connection with the taking of that vote.
I should like to deal with these points calmly and seriatim as they come to my mind. The Minister of Justice blamed the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres because, having this information as to those electoral crimes in his possession for some months, he had not moved the criminal courts of Quebec to arrest and punish those men.
I dio not know whether the MinisieT of Justice meant by his suggestion that my hon. friend should have arrested some 750 men. If he did suggest that I beg ti tell him that a lawyer practising in Montreal cannot contemplate t'he expenditure of some $3,000 for warrants alone as a mere bagatelle. But there is a much more serious reason for my hon. friend having stayed his hand in that connection. The members across the floor of this House, as well as the members on this side, will remember that for some time after the election in this country there was a considerable amount of public excitement, public friction, a feeling between one portion of the country and another, a feeling which I am gilad to say has largely disappeared and is disappearing day by day, and we can thank Heaven for it; but if at that time my hon. friend from Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archam-bault), a French-speaking gentleman from the province of Quebec, had done what the Minister of Justice proposes, and had arrested these English-speaking officers of the

provinces of Ontario and New Brunswick it would have been a very unwise thing to do, and would have caused a lot of hard feeling in this country. Surely the Minister of Justice cannot blame us when we come to him who is supposed to bi the fountain of justice in this country, for redress.
Besides, he did not know until he got the return.

My hon. friend says that he did not know until he got the return, but he had a very shrewd suspicion of these matters. He had not, however, his complete evidence until he obtained it during the session of this Parliament, .and as the Orders of the Day have been pretty well encumbered day by day, I do not think it becomes very highly the Minister of Justice of this department, when a serious matter is brought before him, to meet it by dilatory exceptions or exceptions to the form. Let us go to the very heart and essence o'f this matter, casting aside the juridical niceties about jurisdiction and procedure.
The Minister of Justice says that these articles which appear in Knots and Lashes must be more or less forgiven- that was the inference-because people say harsh things of each other in times of elections. They do, and they have done so in this country, but I am glad to say that never before in Canada have we had such an election as regards bitter attacks as we had last December. I do not think there were very many bitter attacks directed from this side of the House to the other; there may have been some, but I say that for months and months before the last election there was no epithet too grossly insulting to be hurled by the Conservatives or Unionists at the Liberals of this country. The Minister of Justice blames us because he says we circulated the impression throughout this country that the soldiers could cast their votes where they liked. Nothing is more mistaken than that. The soldiers were not free agents at all. But I think there is a good deal of proof in the record, or will be before I have finished the case, that soldiers had to give their votes in many instances, not in all, where their officers who were acting as election officials told them they must vote.
Now I will proceed to discuss why I think this general investigation should be given. First of all, let us look at the soldiers' vote in general. In North America the soldiers' vote amounted to 54,500, and the total votes

rejected amounted to 17,114, or 31i per cent; that is almost one man out of three improperly marked his ballot. How does that fact square with the pretension of the Secretary of State that it was all done by inadvertence, that the people forgot to answer Nos. 6, 7 and 8, or made some other mistake. Does the Secretary of State suggest that we at least on this side of the House have such a low idea of the intellectuality, the mentality, and ability of those men in Canada whose brothers form the finest fighting unit on the Western front as to think that one man out of three marked his ballot improperly by inadvertence? I cannot believe that; I do not believe that. In England-in Great Britain I should say because those of us of Scottish race do not like the old country to be called England; Great Britain is the name which suits us better-in Great Britain 104,377 soldiers votes were cast, and of these 19,251 were rejected, or 18i per cent, and the same argument that I have made in respect to the votes in North America applies, though in not quite so strong a degree, to those votes cast in Great Britain. In France 128,073 votes were cast, and 15,025 were rejected, just about 12i per cent. Is it likely that twelve men out of every hundred more or less improperly marked their ballots in France by inadvertence? I do not think so;
I do not think any member on this side of the House thinks so; I think few members on the other side of the House think so.
And now, if I may be pardoned a personal reference, let me take up the county of Brome, in which I ran, to show how the soldier vote worked out there. Brome is a small agricultural county in the eastern townships. It has no urban centres dignified by the name of "town." The largest village contains about one thousand 'people. Brome had sent some 225 boys to the war, and at the time the vote was taken, from deaths, wounds and discharge, sick- ' ness and discharge, there were not more than 175, or at the most 200, Brome men in the Canadian military forces. Now how many men do you think voted in Brome?
I cannot tell you how many ballots were cast in France to apply in the county of Brome, but 84 were counted, and I presume a large number were rejected. If we take 84 from 200, that leaves 116 Brome men yet to vote. In Great Britain how many Brome men voted? There were 216 votes rejected and 57 votes counted. In Canada there were 112 men voted in Brome. Perhaps I should not have said that men voted in the Old Country, because while my hon. friend from Westmorland was addressing

the House, we learned that some lady was induced by a chaplain to vote, 'in Brome, on the ground that she had "been kind to the Canadian soldiers."
One hundred and twelve men or women voted in Canada under the provisions of the Military Voters Act in the county of Bronio. If we take the same proportion for the votes cast in France as for the votes cast in England-and of course these figures are in the possession of the Government and they cbm verify everything I say-you will find that about three times the number of men who were in the army at the time of the election voted in the little county of Brome. Had all these votes been counted, the splendid majority the people gave me, the largest majority which was ever given in the county of Brome at a really fought out election, a majority of 609, would have been wiped out and I would not have had the pleasure of meeting hon. members on the other side of the House.
Bet me deal, in connection with the vote in Great Britain with the argument advanced by the hon. the Secretary of State (Mr. Burrell) that if a few mistakes were made, they were merely mistakes and inadvertences. I nave a copy of the list which has been certified to by Mr. Fraser and Mr. Soles. Mr. Fraser was the special returning officer and Mr. Soles was his clerk. I do not know Mr. Fraser but Mr. Soles is a gentleman occupying a responsible position in the Civil Service. He is a well known civil servant and he was sent to France for the purpose of counting the vote. I think he is one of the inspectors engaged in laying out rural mail routes, he has his headquarters in Sherbrooke, and he is a perfectly responsible gentleman. I wish to state that the punse was not made away with, that I still retain my seat which I won, and that the 216 men whose votes were rejected failed to answer questions, 6, 7 and 8. Where did these gentlemen come from? Were they all gentlemen who came from the old country and who had a right under the Military Voters Act to apply their votes in whatever county they wished? No. I do not propose to read a long list of these men. I have not the address of every one of them but from the investigations which have been made, and the examination of the rolls of the regiments, it was ascertained that 62 of them came from counties, stretching, to use the expression frequently employed by orators in this county, from the stormy waves of the Atlantic to the calm waters of the Pacific.
Spare us.

Perhaps I should. As it is getting late I will endeavour to be as brief as possible. Out of the 62 names on this list investigated only one belonged to the county of Brome, a man called Plouff, who came originally from Sutton and who bad become a United States citizen.
Now let us come to the question of the vote in Canada. 112 votes were cast outside of the county of Brome, for the county of Brome. Of those 56 were counted and 56 were rejected. We have a record of how the questions were answered by those 56. Some 40 answered to the effect that they had resided in Canada at the time of their enlistment, but like those poor, unfortunate forgetful fellows in the barracks at St. Johns, Quebec, they did not Ijnow where they had ever lived in Canada, or they could not say where they had lived in Canada. Some 40 or so answered the questions. Others who had tenderer consciences or had not been so well coached answered questions that they lived in Canada at the time of their enlistment and then did not answer 6, 7 and 8 and applied their vote to Brome. Does any hon. gentleman on the other side of the House desire me or any member to believe that these votes were cast by inadvertence or by a strange coincidence in the county of Brome? No, I will tell you why I was picked out for slaughter from the first. I do not think that I am a particularly bad man; at least my badness has not made me notorious. I was picked out for slaughter by this Union Government because I was running in one of the two essentially English-speaking constituencies in Quebec, where the population is English yet by a very considerable majority. In the county of Brome. about two-thirds of the voters are English-speaking and about one-third French-speaking. The population is divided about 60 per cent English and about 40 per cent French. The difference between the voting strength and the population is due to the fact that there are a great number of people whose children have left them to go to out West or to go into the city of Montreal, and a great number of French Canadians with large families of children have come into the county in comparatively recent years. I was picked out for slaughter because this Union Government did not wanj, it to be shown that there was an English-speaking county in Quebec that could be carried for Laurier and the straight, grand old Liberal party. They failed, and if I speak with some warmth about this matter it is because I think I have a right to. I ran as clean a campaign

in the county as any man ever ran in the Dominion. I had as my opponent a gallant and distinguished soldieT across the seas. What did this party, that includes the best elements in both political parties, do? They stuck placards on every barn door and on every rock in Brome saying, "Draper is fighting the Hun, McMiaster is fighting Draper; for whom would the Kaiser vote?" The old, old Tory trick, to endeavour to pretend that they have a monopoly of the patriotism of the country and any one who does not agree with them is not patriotic. I ask why the soldiers voted as they did? I ask why there were so many irregularties committed' in connection with the soldiers' vote tooth in Canada and across the sea. I will tell you; it was on account of the campaign of misrepresentation and abuse that this Union Government put up in the last general election. Let me just rehearse very briefly why the people of Canada lost their heads in the last general election. On the first day of December the Prime Minister made a speech in a certain western Ontario town and 'was not very well received. And the next- day there was held in Toronto, at the house of a very godly gentleman there, a meeting of some tw'enty people, who were very prominent in Y.M.
C.A. work, and who were also endowed with a goodly portion of this world's goods. Diligence in business was united with fervour of spirit, and these gentlemen who protested that they were followers of the God of love made up their minds that the Ontario farmer was in a very difiieult and uncomfortable frame of mind for- the Unionist party and that something must be done. And out of that meeting there came a committee-out of that meeting, or similar meetings, out of that class of men there came a Citizens' Union 'Committee. These men, who said they were followers of the God of love, went out for the purpose of winning an election, to sow hate between different sections of our Canadian people. Was there ever more horrid, hideous and odious hypocrisy? I do not think there has been. These men-I wish they were within the sound of my voice-are familiar with the history of the Founder of our religion. They know that although He dismissed with a kindly word the poor woman taken in flagrant sin, that although He forgave the penitent thief on the cross, He preserved the vials of His righteous indignation for those whom He called scribes, and Pharisees, and hypocrites, those who liked to broaden their phylacteries and stand at the corners of the streets making long prayers to be seen of all-these men 
went out, and this is the sort of stuff they spread through the papers of Ontario:
Is a united Quebec to rule all Canada?
The glaring advertisement in which this appeared had the Union Jack and the British, lion prominently displayed at eadh of its four corners.
To-day in our national crisis Quebec along among all the provinces stands more united than ever before. She knows what she wants:
(1)	Withdrawal from the war.
A downright lie as black as any that ever came from the abode of the father of lies himself.
(2)	'Bilingual schools everywhere.
(3)	Weakening of the ties of British connection.
(4)	Political control of Canada.
Political control of Canada! As if one province of >a population of a little over two millions could control other provinces whose aggregate population amounted to six millions. And listen, Mr. Speaker, to this gem :
Within the last few weeks, Quebec has mobilized all her forces to dominate Canada under the unified leadership of Bourassa and Laurier.
The united leadership of Bourassa and Laurier. Why, if there has been one man in the province of Quebec, who, for the last forty years, has been standing four-square against the prejudices of his province it is my revered, and honoured, and beloved leader, Sir Wilfrid Laurier. The Montreal Weekly Witness well said that such a statement was effrontery worthy of the Prussian general staff. But they had another untruth to tell about those people who did not agree with him politically:
All Canada knows that Germany has been working through agents, spies and bribes in every country in the world. The latest evidences are the revelations recently made to the world iby President Wilson. Do we Canadians think the Kaiser has overlooked Canada? If we do, what a fool's paradise!
Now, I have in my hand the Ottawa Evening Journal of Monday, December 10, 1917, and this paragraph appears in all its wicked untruthfulness in full in that paper. But in the Ottawa Citizen of about the same date I find that the last most odious statement and inference that German gold was being used at the last election is left out.
I do mot know who is responsible for it. Perhaps this was a little too strong for the Citizen's stomach, although the Journal was able to swallow it. There is something I want to say-I think it should he said, although it may not be agreeable to say it:
I have no quarreil with people who believe

that their political duty obliged them to join the Union Cabinet, because they considered that conscription was a large enough and broad enough issue upon which to base a government. It always struck me, Mr. Speaker, that conscription was a very narrow platform on which men of different political traditions and different political outlooks should get together, because, after all, it is a matter of procedure, and the somewhat interesting thing is that the conscription law on which these gentlemen joined together has been, by their own declaration, practically admitted a failure, and they have had to change the very essence of their law and get rid of the selective feature which characterized it. But I have no quarrel with any one who joined that Government because he sincerely thought it was his duty, to do so-I respect the convictions of all. I have expressed what I think of this sort of thing:
The Citizen's Union Committee. A NonPartisan War-Time Organization to Support Union Government. J. W. Lyon, Guelph, Chairman ; Norman Sommerville, Toronto, ViceChairman ; G. A. Warburton, Chairman Executive Committee; Albert H. Abbott, Secretary.
G. A. Warburton is a name, if I mistake not, I have seen connected with the prohibition movement in the province of Ontario, and also with Y. M. C. A. campaigns in the same province. That sort of thing is just the very worst and most wicked thing that we could have in Canada, and that was spread abroad throughout Ontario in both Liberal and Conservative papers. I asked myself this question: Did the leader of the. Unionist party in Ontario try to stop that sort of thing, or did he profit by it? Because if he profited by it, if'he allowed that to go unchallenged, and if he did not do everything he could to stop that sort of thing he did wrong. I am willing to pause to find out from him now whether he tried to stop that sort of thing, because I do not want to accuse him unjustly and I await his reply.
He will not reply.

No answer. I do not
want to say anything that would not be fair and right to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell). What did the President of the Privy Council do in this campaign that was going on? He went up to North Bay and made a bitter attack upon the French Catholic orders that had come to this country.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if his words were true, I would not have very much to say. I
would permit myself, perhaps, to criticise the wisdom, in an election of this sort, of raising a personal attack upon those Orders 'of a religion to which I did not belong. I think that would be fair criticism. But the President of the Council, eight weeks ago, was told in the most firm and unmistakable manner, and with proofs, that his assertion was incorrect. And although we have had a statement handed out to the press, which is, possibly, a new way in which men belonging to this- Government answer their adversaries-or some of them;
I don't want to be unfair to those who use the old fashioned way and come into the House to make their own defence- eight weeks have passed without reply; and except for this statement handed out to the press, we have had no statement from the President of the Council either adducing the proof that he was right when he made those charges or that he withdraws them like a man.
Now, you may ask, why should I say this, what object have I? I have no desire to hurt the feelings of the President of the Council. I admire his ability and his devotion to the public service; he is a hardworking man. I say it for this purpose: that very shortly the President of the Council is going over to the old land, and I do not want him to represent himself as a Liberal there, as a sort of modern George Brown, who has joined a Union Government for the sake of saving Canada. I think I know what you are looking at, Mr. Speaker. You are wondering whether I am keeping to the motion. And therefore I have said all I need to say on that question. With his usual acumen and nimbleness of mind, the President of the Council knows exactly what I mean. I will see his career in the Tory party with pleasure, but I do not want him to represent himself as a Liberal.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I hope the hon. member will confine his remarks more closely to the subject.
I will, Mr. Speaker, and I thank you for your indulgence. Now, have I made out a case, Mr. Speaker?
No, not yet.

I was addressing my remarks to the Speaker. Have I made out a case, Mr. Speaker, for a general investigation? I believe I have. It will be for the Government now to grant an investigation now, or not to grant an investigation. And if they are successful in getting their followers to vote against their desire

. and against their will for the maintenance of the power of creating life titles in Canada, I do not know how the vote will go, but I leave it before the House.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. L. SIFTON (Minister of Customs) :
speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not going to detain the House very long at this , time of the morning in regard to the discussion of the election that took place on the 17th December last, and which, for the first time, we are discussing this evening in this House. I have been a little disappointed, in connection with this matter. Having for a great many years taken an academic interest in the conduct of the affairs of the Dominion of Canada, I have noticed that, after every general election, in the debate on the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne, or the very first available opportunity in the House, the members of the Opposition, whichever that Opposition might happen to be at that particular time, devoted the greater part of the first session to showing the country that they had obtained a moral victory. That has been the custom ever since Confederation; and here we have waited now for two or three months, and to-night is practically the first time that it has been brought to your attention, Mr. Speaker, that the members of the Opposition obtained a moral victory in December, 1917.
The reason that has been brought to your attention to-night is peculiar. A gentleman has just arrived from England with the * evidence, according to the first speaker in this debate, which has proved that the Opposition obtained a victory, or should have obtained a victory, if they had had their rights. They ignore absolutely-and it is absurd to discuss the question-that the people of Canada, utterly regardless of all the soldiers' votes, returned the supporters of this Government by a very considerable majority. They ignore the fact that if they consulted the figures they would probably find that if all the soldiers had not voted at all, or if in the bulk of the constituencies they had all voted against this Government, the result would have been very much the same in a great number of cases. These things are absolutely immaterial to the members of the Opposition in connection with this matter. They are not so much material to them as they are to the particular member who last addressed you in regard to this, because he has taken a low stand, as if a gentleman of his eminence and ability, representing an English-speaking constituency in the Province of Quebec, should not

receive any opposition from the members of this side.
Mr. MoMASTER: No.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: I have had some part in elections for a great many years, and I have always proceeded upon the basis that every member of the Opposition and every supporter of the Government should be opposed honestly to the best strength that all the members of these respective parties have, and no member has a right to get up and say that he received special attention and that was made an object to defeat him. They did not succeed to do it in all; nor in the County of Brome they did not' succeed. And they did not succeed, because, as the hon. gentleman has shown, the officers of this Government, whom he now blamed for not taking part properly in the conduct of this election, threw out the soldiers' votes that he says would have defeated him if they had been counted. And because the officials in the conduct of the election carried out their duty as it was carried out, because a number of soldiers' votes that were improperly cast either in England or in. Canada were thrown out by the officials of this Government, and the member for Brome was elected by the resident voters of that di = trict, therfore he says that he was the subject of special attack and singled out to be defeated. Apparently the gentlemen who were in charge of the campaign either in Toronto or otherwise were not competen' for their job.
Something slipped.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
They apparently succeeded in a great many places in accomplishing what they were for, but they fell down in the constituency of Brome. And, as a consequence, Mr. Speaker, we have the privilege of listening to the address we have had to-night. And the hon. member for Brome forgets all about the soldiers, he forgets about the importance that it is to the Dominion of Canada to see that there is an investigation into the conduct of soldiers abroad; he forgets the important things that were mentioned by the first gentleman who moved this resolution in regard to the effect on the country. He devoted,the greater part of his speech to a political address in opposition to the people of Toronto and to the President of the Council. What has this to do with the motion with which the member for Westmorland has occupied the time of the House in connection with the vote of the soldiers overseas? As a supporter of this -

Government and as a private member of this House, I am opposed to any judicial investigation of what took place in England and in France in connection with the soldiers' vote. Every one knew when the War-time Elections Act was passed-any one^who did not know should have known -that it was impossible in a time of war to take the vote of the soldiers overseas in the same manner that the civilian vote at home is taken. Every one recognized the fact that you could not pass a law making perjury in England perjury in Canada; that you could not pass an Elections Act that could be enforced in England and France as it could in the constituency of Brome, for instance, or any other constituency of Canada. When Parliament passed that law they left it to the honour of the soldiers to vote in accordance with the dictates of their consciences and in what they believed to be the best interests of their country. If Parliament could not trust the soldiers, they had no right to provide for the taking of the vote overseas, because under no circumstances can the soldiers in France and England be made subject to the same rules that are applicable to an election in this country. Either the matter had to be left to the honour of the soldiers, or the' soldiers had to be left without votes. At the last session Parliament chose the other course; they gave the votes to the soldiers overseas, and so far as I have been able to discover, the Election was carried out as well as it could possibly be carried out under the circumstances.
We are told that the soldiers were in-' fluenced by their officers. Hon. gentlemen who make that suggestion know perfectly well that the soldiers did not need to be influenced by their officers. Only to-night a man who has just come from there and who was present in one of the units on the occasion of the election told me that three soldiers in that unit who desired to vote for the Opposition, and did so, immediately asked to be locked up in the guard-room in order to escape from their comrades who unitedly supported Union Government. It .was not necessary for the officers to issue any instructions; the privates would have risen in rebellion against them if the officers had not allowed them to vote as they did vote, almost unanimously, for the Government pledged to carry on the war to the very utmost of its ability. That is the view I take with regard to this matter; that is the view which I believe will be taken throughout the length and breadth of
Canada and by the vast majority of the members of this House.

speakeroldname: Rt. Hon. Sir GEORGE FOSTER (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
I do not want to trespass at length upon the time of the House, and I shall confine myself to a very few minutes. Most of the ground has been traversed well by my three colleagues who have spoken on this side of the House, but there are two or three points that I think we might touch upon before the vote is taken.
There is a saying-it is hardly a saying, for it consists of only two Latin words,- which has come to me out of the degree of my former Latinity, whatever 1 may have possessed. I refer to the expression "cui bono"-to what good purpose? These words have been on my mind all the time during which this debate has been going on, and they were running through my head more rapidly during the speech of the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster). Viewing the matter in the light of the present situation, in the light of this gathering of 200 busy men from every part of the Dominion of Canada, in the dying day of the session, with the weight and the burdens of the war in their hearts, upon their minds and on their shoulders, and in the light of the duties awaiting them at home,-to what earthly good the speech that was made by the member for Brome? Let each one try to answer that question. As the Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Sifton) said, my hon. friend drifted entirely from the impersonal question of the soldier and the war, and made the mistake that a young preacher often makes: That of putting himself in the front and not getting behind the pith and essence of the gospel which he is preaching. My hon. friend did not add to the weight of moral tone or the firmness of moral fibre in this country when he-held up to the ridicule of this House? no; he could not do that; this House is a little hit too serious to look upon it as a matter of ridicule-but >when 'he attempted to hold up to the ridicule of this House men such as he mentioned as forming a committee in Toronto or in Ontario. Cui bono, to single out worthy Christian workers in any line-the Y.M.C.A., or workers on behalf of prohibition, temperance or any other good cause. Why single them out and hold them up to the scorn of a hundred or two hundred men and to the scorn and the laughter, if he is able to provoke it, of the people of the country? We have none too much of this moral fibre in our country, and I never like to hear a man chiding or

jeering at men whose chief object in life
is doing Christ's work in the way they com sider to be the most honourable and the most effective way of doing it. Cui bono? Is it an aimless curiosity that prompts such talk as we have had here to-day? It is curiosity to look into the workings of a watch and to tear it to pieces, to see how the wheels go around, well knowing that it is an old watch which will never be used to keep time again. I can see that there would be some purpose in having an investigation into the methods of the election in England and France if that mode of election were ever supposed to be used again 'in choosing the members of the Parliament of Canada. But that method of selection has been forced upon us by a great war. It would never have been possible under other circumstances, and we hope that it will never be used again because it is made necessary by another great war. It would be infinitely interesting and amusing to my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) if he knew exactly everything that took place in the trenches when soldiers were voting, how they were led to vote and everything like that. But cui bono? Where is he going to apply it as a lesson to aid and help, for the, good of this country or of his own constituency? May I say to my hon, friend that when, as he well observed in the early portion of . his remarks, there was a change in the relations of peoples and sections of peoples in Canada at the present time, as compared with what was the condition six months ago, twelve months ago, more or less-what earthly good would it be to bring again into the arena and fight at the old causes of separation and dissention, and renew, 'so far as he could pour oil upon the fire, the smoke and the flame of a contest and conflagration which we were all hoping had died] down never to be relighted again-? To what good again, I say? No argument has been given here this evening at all to show that, if all those investigations were carried on and all the information was gathered, there would be one iota of change in the parties, and the policies, and the principles, which govern this country as a result of the election of the 17th of December, 1917.' There is no national political interest in the matter at all, because no amount of investigation could! ever cause any change in the policies and principles being carried on in this country at the present time. I think this is a fair method of criticism. There were several things which could have been done. But just now the thought comes to my mind'-to 
what good! again? There are in this country, people who. do mot like the war, people who do not care much for our soldiers, some people-il hope there are not very many-who roll under their tongue as a sweet morsel anything which will derogate from the war party, from the soldier, from that portion, that effort of the Dominion of Canada which is behind this war and is pushing it to the conclusion to which it must be pushed if we are to keep our lives and liberties and status intact. Does it help to throw the blur and fog and mist and darkness of mistakes that have been committed by soldiers, if mistakes have been committed; of irregularities that have been committed by soldiers or officers, if irregularities have been committed? Does it help in the united purpose of this Dominion of Canada that such should be dug up and thrown out? I do not think it does. I have, flashing before my mind just now, two illustrations of that in the history of the present war. Galipoli and Mesopotamia were dark features in the campaigns of the last two or three years. There were allegations; there were thoughts; there were ideas; there were even facts which in normal times would have carried like a whirlwind investigation of the very keenest and deepest kind. Great Britain did not investigate. The war was on, and nothing was done which would dim the public ardour, nothing which would tend to make confusion or disorder or lack of unity and purpose in the carrying on of the w-ar, either as affecting Great Britain herself or her standing and that of the army and that of the war in the -view of the warring enemy. So, many things that otherwise would have been looked into have been left over until the war is at an und. Will it <Io any good at all for us to fling out a drag-net investigation into soldiers, lieutenants and captains, and with that dragnet proceed through Great Britain, and, if we are logical, through France as well and elsewhere? Will it help in any way? To what good again? It is a matter which appeals to my mind as being one of infinitesimal importance in comparison with the great purpose for which we are handed together and which this country is doing its very best to carry out.
There is close at hand an element which has been imported into this discussion. My hon. friend from Chatnbly and Ver-cheres ('Mr. Archambault) had three courses before him. He has chosen one. He has ignored the other two. There was one course,-I do not know whether this

course is politically possible or not. He has had the knowledge of what he calls irregularities and if his statements are proved, if the prima facie evidence turns out to be true evidence, he has made statements which reflect upon the honour of soldiers and which involve strongly a moral question. One course open to him would have been to come with his information the very first moment he got it and lay it before the Government and ask them to deal with it and make such investigations and mete cut such discipline as they thought possible. My hon. friend smiles-that is not the party way of doing such things; that would not have had the effect for him nor for his party that he hopes has been had by the method of procedure which he did ultimately adopt. But I take it that, in many a case, in grave situations like this, the quiet way of scotching an evil and preventing it from spreading is the best way, and that was one way open to my hon. friend. But he did not'take it. There was not enough light and shadow about that. There was another way. The moment that the hon. gentleman got into this House, the moment that the House came together, why should he not, burdened with all that information which showed to his mind dire and dreadful iniquity, the influence of which could not be good for soldier or for national life, bring that information and put it upon the table of the House and press for an investigation early in the session when the House would have had an opportunity of dealing with the matter? Instead of doing that, he waits until the day before the House is to prorogue and then on an independent motion he and his confreres bring those matters and chuck them into the House. Such a motion, under those circumstances, no Government could .allow to pass. In spite of all the camouflage and smoke screens that may be thrown up, there is no possibility, on a motion such as this of a discussion which would be fair or an investigation which would be thorough by a Committee of the House or by the House .itself in any capacity. One of those two courses he could have taken, but he has taken a third. I am only criticising the method.

Is my hon. friend not aware that on the I6th of April I put a question on the Order Paper asking for the production of documents, which, if received, would have enabled me to move for this inquiry .earlier?
.156

My hon. friend put on the Order Paper questions which if they had been .answered or could have been answered would have .enabled him to bring in two sets of information; first, the information that he has read out as to where these men were bom, where they enlisted, their residence .and the like of that. He had the sworn .affidavits of his own men .as to that in his pocket all the time. Men of his own ctioosing, in whom he had confidence bad furnished him with the prima facie case he has put before the House to-day. That was made a little stronger by the documents which he did get. I take leave to ,say that the stand taken by the Minister of Justice, which the Government has stuck to, was the fair thing, namely, that it is not the right of any person to go in and take hold, for any purpose whatsoever, of the documents which are the records of the elections of the country, .and which are guarded as great secrets. They can be brought out for use in a judicial commission or in an investigation by a Committee of the House, if they are ordered, but it is irregular, and it would lead to dire consequence's if these documents could be fished into for information at any time and every person. So I say that my hon. friend having .sufficient evidence, evidence of his own choosing, furnished by his own scrutineers in whom he had confidence and who had charge of his election, if he had laid it before the House at an earlier period of the session, it would have brought the House to a discussion of the matter under such conditions as would make it a real discussion and would enable a conclusion to be come to by the House on the merits of the case. But to throw into the House to-day, as has been done, a vast mass of stuff that took four hours and a little better to read-how can a Government or how can the House itself make any valuation. of these things? A thousand and one incidents may have to be probed in order to test whether those things are worthy of an investigation or not. However that may be, the matter has come before the House; the Government has met it, and the Minister of Justice and my other colleagues have spoken in detail to the House.
I have but one thing more to say. The moral quality in the question which has been raised by my hon. friend from Cham-bly and Vercheres is a different phase of the matter. To- what good may well be asked with reference to the other phases I have discussed, because they are ephemeral; they cannot have any very .great advantage as a guide for future action. But moral



delinquency stands on a different plane. The moral question was what was raised by my hon. friend from Chambly and Ver-cheres, and that cannot be ignored by any House of Parliament or by any Government. With reference to that, while I am not going to say on prima facie evidence that officers of the militia or military formations of this country have done anything that is dishonourable or wrong-we cannot say that until the matter is investigated-I am bound to say that when things of that kind come before the House the Government and the House itself must take cognizance of them, 'because the moral quality is one which pervades the community to-day and pervades it always, and it must be kept as pure and as strong and as elevated as we can possibly keep it. And so when evidence of that kind is put before it the Government is prepared to say-it could not do less-that it will be probed to the very bottom, and that in so far as the evidence goee to show wrongdoing, the wrongdoing will be punished, even though we may be sorry in our very heart of hearts that such things do occur and have to be made examples of. The Government purposes to do that.
My hon. friend from Brome (Mr. MiMas-ter) started out with the idea that he could put up as direct a case as was put up by my hon. friend from Obambly and Ver-cheres, but he forgot his case in attending to himself, and so he put up no case for an investigation.
As to a general dragnet thrown over this country in one of the crises of our country's efforts impugning the whole military organization of Canada, putting it under suspicion and having it menaced by the coming investigation, whether anything has been proved or not in the first case, no man of good common sense would think that a good thing to help on the war at the present time. But we will take this particular case, and it will be looked into thoroughly and speedily, and as the evidence is brought forth so will the punishment rest on individuals who have been guilty of wrong-doing. The Government must go on; we must have our Supply, and we must stand by the motion to go into Committee of Supply. That, I believe, is a sensible thing to do, and that is what I think will be done when the vote is taken.
Sir WILFRhD LAURIER: Mr. Speaker, we have heard from four ministers, and now the motion comes at last to' what we might have expected; the Government take it as a motion of want of confidence. Now

an amendment to the motion to go into Committee of Supply is a motion of want of confidence if the Government wauts to make it a motion of want of confidence, and it is not a motion of want of confidence if the Government does not choose to make it so. Again and again in this House amendments have been made to the motion to go into Committee of Supply by members of the Opposition, and again and again Conservative governments and Liberal Governments have accepted those motions, and not treated them as motions of want of confidence.
Those occasions are exceedingly rare.

Such cases
have occurred in the Government of which my hon. friend was a member. I remember a case in the eighties, when my hon. friend was a member of the Government of Sir John A. Macdonald, on a motion for 'Supply Mr. Mills, the member for Bothwell, moved an amendteient that public buildings should not be built except in. places where the revenue justified it. Sir John Macdonald accepted the motion at once, as it was a proper motion. He did not treat it as a motion of want of confidence, and my hon. friend assented to it also. I can remember a case in which the Government of which -I was the head accepted an amendment to the motion for Supply moved by Sir Charles Tupper and seconded' by my right hon. friend (Sir George Foster).
I suppose my right hon. friend's memory will carry him back to the occasions where he refused it over and over again.

Only yesterday a motion was made in this House, as to the merits of which every one was agreed, but the Government chose to take it as a motion of want of confidence.
But the Government made this a party question, and therefore everybody has to bow. Yesterday the Government was concerned. They had just passed an Order in iCouncil which to a certain extent negatived the motion, and then wanted their supporters to stand by them. But in this case the Government are not involved. Neither my hon. friend who moved the motion, nor my hon. friend who seconded it, accused the Government. They made charges of wrong-doing. In those charges the Government are not concerned. Up to the present time not one word has been said against the Government. Will the

Government step in and have an investigation? No, they say, we will not grant this inquiry, we will make it a party question, and therefore every follower apparently will have to do what he did yesterday, swallow his convictions and support the Government.
My right hon. friend (Sir George Foster) stated a lot of objections to this motion. It comes too late; why did it not come earlier? My right hon. friend asked my hon. friend from Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault) why he did not bring this matter to the Government. Whoever heard of a matter of this kind being brought to the Government. This is the great inquest of the nation, this is the place where all accusations are brought, and I will ask my right hon. friend, if he will permit me, if he ever heard of an accusation of this kind going to the Government? Did he ever hear of it? Such a thing never took place. It is a phantom of the imagination of the right hon. gentleman to try and bolster up a bad case.
Then my hon. friend from Chambly-Vercheres was asked by the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) why he did not take this to the courts of law. He might have accused somebody of wrongdoing. He certainly might have done so, but does any one pretend that when such grave charges are brought to the attention of the House as those which my hon. friend from Chambly-Verchbres has placed before us to-night, that justice would have been done to the public if there had been an appeal to the courts of law? Some parties might have been punished. But what we want is not to punish parties, but to uphold and vindicate the honour and dignity of the law. That is why this motion is made. My right hon. friend told us that even if the charges were true no national interests would be served by an investigation. Let me answer at once that we know we cannot change the complexion of this Parliament, and such is not our intention. But, is the matter confined to that? Does my right hon. friend pretend that when an election has taken place, as it took place under the circumstances of the last election, the honour of the country is not a? consideration, that the law of the land is not a consideration, and that we are not interested to know whether or not the law has been observed? It is not to change the complexion of this House, it is not to change the Government, but it is to maintain the principle of the electoral law of the land, without which there is no liberty whatever.
We are fighting to-day for liberty. That is our pride, but will my right hon. friend tell me that, when we are fighting for liberty to-day, if such charges as these are brought they should not be investigated? These charges are either true or they are not true -I think they are-but we do not condemn anybody. We simply ask that the Government should have an opportunity to have an investigation, in order to find out whether these charges are true or not. It is not necessary to tell us that there are no national interests involved. It is the honour of the land that is involved. It is more than that. It is the foundation of the institutions under which we live. If there is anything that is sacred in this country, or wherever British institutions exist, it is the freedom of elections and the sanctity of the vote. That is what is at stake to-day. We are told that we should not vote for this motion. It is a principle of British justice, a principle of British institutions, that whenever and wherever a crime has been committed, no matter what it is, that crime must be investigated. If I find on the wayside a dead body, it is my duty to notify immediately -an officer of the law; the coroner comes, empanels the jury, summons witnesses, and leaves no stone unturned, until the murderer is discovered, and justice is done. It is the same thing here. The principle of electoral freedom lies prostrate, killed in the House of its own . friends, and this is simply a coroner's inquest called to inquire into the matter so that the culprits may be brought to justice.

Hon. F. B. CARVELL moved that the amendments made by the Senate to Bill No. 41 to amend the Navigable Waters Protection Act be read the second time and concurred in.
What are the amendments in question?

As the Bill was drafted it provided that the Minister of Public Works alone should have the right to say what works might be forcibly removed from the navigable streams, and also that he alone should have the right to state what works might be placed in the stream. When we came to examine the situation we found that the harbours of Montreal and Vancouver, and wherever there are harbour commissions, are really under the control of the Marine and Fisheries Department. Therefore when the Bill went to the Senate we had its provisions changed, otherwise it would have taken away from that department their jurisdiction over those national harbours.
Motion agreed to.

It is not distributed yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Some copies were distributed this morning. The purpose of the Bill is merely to amend the Banking Act to provide that a bill of exchange may be protested at half past two in the afternoon instead of three o'clock. It is a great convenience to the bankers, and d'oes no harm to any one.
Has it the fiat of the Bankers'' Association?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It has been asked for by the Bankers' Association. I move the second reading of the Bill.

Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time.
The House went into committee on the Bill, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1:
What will the public think of this change?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It merely makes a man's note subject to protest half an hour sooner than it otherwise would be. A very large number of young men have voluntarily enlisted from the staffs of the banks and others are taken under the Military Service Act. If the banks are obliged to defer action until three o'clock in the afternoon, they have to keep their staffs, now greatly reduced, working very late.
Is this intended to be permanent?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Only during the war, and a year after.
Suppose a man's note was protested at half past two and the bank is open for deposit until three? He might expect by three o'clock to have money in the bank to cover the note?

It is proposed that the banks shall close during the period of the war at half past two o'clock. The banks might d'o that without any amendment to the Banking Act, but the Act provides that obligations not paid cannot be protested until three; and that is the purpose of the change.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.
